#5407. The professions Americans trust the most — and least

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Doctors, scientists, and teachers earn the most trust in a 31-country survey, while politicians and influencers sit at the bottom of 20 groups.

A patient fills a prescription on a doctor's word. A parent signs a field trip form because a teacher vouched for the outing. A voter hears a campaign pledge and weighs whether to believe it. Each of these moments turns on a quiet judgment about whether the person on the other side deserves credence. Professionals shape the health care people receive, the schooling their children get, the money they save, the laws they live under, and the news they read. Most people cannot check that work for themselves. Few patients can audit a diagnosis, and few savers can inspect a bank's books. Faith in expertise fills the space between what people know and what they must accept, and it steers everyday choices large and small.

Public confidence splinters across these roles. Some occupations command broad goodwill, and others draw open suspicion. The divide runs through single fields and single institutions, where two jobs that share a label can land far apart in public esteem. A broad tag such as "business" or "government" can hide those splits, and anyone reading the popular mood through one catchall word risks missing them. Approval and doubt coexist. A single job can win praise from one slice of the population and scorn from another, and a tally of supporters on its own misses the balance between the two camps. Measuring how far trust outruns distrust, or the reverse, tells a clearer story about where each line of work stands.

Visual Capitalist ranked 20 professions and groups by that balance, using data from the Ipsos Global Trustworthiness Index 2026. Ipsos polled 23,537 adults online across 31 countries, with fieldwork running from June 19 to July 3, 2026. Respondents judged whether each profession or group in their own country was trustworthy or untrustworthy. Net trust, the measure behind the ranking, subtracts the share who chose untrustworthy from the share who chose trustworthy and expresses the result in percentage points. A group that 50% of respondents call trustworthy and 30% call untrustworthy, for example, would earn a net score of +20. The figure captures the margin of trust over distrust. It does not represent the share of people who trust the group. A positive score shows trust outweighing distrust, and a negative score signals the opposite. Each of the 31 countries carries equal weight in the averages, so the results do not form a global estimate scaled to population. The published figures leave the countries unnamed and offer no results for any one of them.

Doctors claim the highest net trust of all 20 groups in the survey, at +43 points. They belong to the health and knowledge category, a cluster that also takes in scientists, teachers, and personal trainers. Among adults polled across 31 countries, no other occupation drew a wider margin of confidence over doubt.

A 91-point gulf separates doctors from politicians, who post -48 at the opposite end of the list. Visual Capitalist calls the distance stark. No two groups stand farther apart, so the doctor-politician pairing marks the full width of public opinion the index captures.

Skepticism toward politicians runs deeper than goodwill toward doctors. Politicians sink 48 points below zero, and doctors climb 43 points above it. The bottom figure outweighs the top one by five points in magnitude, which suggests the survey's harshest verdict carries more force than its warmest endorsement.

Doctors hold a 27-point margin over the armed forces at +16. Every group outside the health and knowledge category, from judges and police to bankers and journalists, falls behind physicians by at least that distance.

Personal trainers, a fellow health and knowledge group, register +10, a full 33 points beneath doctors. A shared category label does not guarantee a shared standing with the public. The health label cannot account for the doctors' edge, because a group in the same field lags them by a wider gap than the one separating doctors from the armed forces.

Scientists hold a net trust score of +42 points, one point behind doctors and second among the 20 groups in the survey. A gap of a single point at the head of the list amounts to a near tie. Adults across the 31 countries rate researchers almost level with the physicians who treat them.

Doctors, scientists, and teachers fill the three highest positions in 27 of the 31 countries surveyed, according to Ipsos. Four countries depart from that order. The trio's grip across so many countries shows the standing of scientists does not hinge on a few outliers in the combined average.

Teachers, the third member of that trio, trail scientists by five points at +37. The one-point margin separating scientists from doctors is a fifth the size of that cushion. The summit of the list plays out as a two-way contest, with teachers a step back.

Scientists stand 90 points above politicians, the group with the lowest score of the 20. Nearly the full spread of opinion in the survey separates the people who conduct research from the people who seek elected office.

This slide runs about 185 words, below the 300-word minimum. The source supplies only the scientists' +42 net trust score, their second-place position, and the Ipsos finding that doctors, scientists, and teachers hold the top three spots in 27 of 31 countries. It gives no reasons, country names, demographics, or trends for scientists, and no approved web detail covers scientists, so the slide stops where the evidence ends instead of padding.

Vocabulary flag: "trust," "points," "scientists," and "countries" recur across paragraphs because no precise synonym exists for the measure, the subject, or the survey scope.

Teachers carry net trust of +37 points, good for third among the 20 groups, and they finish 21 points ahead of the armed forces at +16. No other pair of neighbors on the list sits so far apart. Each remaining step between adjacent groups in the top 10 covers six points or fewer. The steepest drop near the bottom, from clergy/priests at -11 to advertising executives at -26, spans 15 points and falls short of the teacher divide. Advertising executives and government ministers, 11 points apart, form the next-widest pair.

The step down from teachers covers more ground than the entire climb from the first negative score, held by pollsters at -2, up to the armed forces. The 18-point stretch between those marks holds seven groups, counting both ends, including personal trainers, tech entrepreneurs, judges, police, and lawyers. Police and pollsters, whose scores straddle zero, sit seven points apart, one-third the size of the gap below teachers.

Teachers trail doctors by six points and scientists by five. The three Health and knowledge groups fit inside a six-point band at the summit. Below them, the armed forces post a score less than half the mark teachers earn. Teachers outscore the combined total of the three groups beneath them. The armed forces, personal trainers, and tech entrepreneurs add up to +31, six points under the teacher figure.

Shared category membership offers no guarantee of a high finish. Personal trainers, the fourth Health and knowledge group, land at +10, which leaves them 27 points behind teachers. The gulf between teachers and politicians, who sit at -48, stretches to 85 points. Government ministers register -37, the exact inverse of the teacher score. Educators enjoy a margin of confidence as wide as the margin of doubt ministers face.

Read together, the gaps describe a list that splits into a leading trio and everyone else, with teachers guarding the boundary.

The armed forces hold net trust of +16 points, the strongest showing of any group outside the health and knowledge category. Doctors, scientists, and teachers, the only groups above the military, all work in medicine, research, or education. The military is the first public institution on the list, in fourth place, and the only group beyond health and knowledge to reach double digits.

The armed forces open a wide margin over the three other groups that share the public institutions label. Judges and police each reach +5, leaving the military 11 points clear of both. Government officials and civil servants slip to -9, 25 points below the armed forces' mark. Across those four groups, the category stretches from solid confidence to outright doubt, with the uniformed service at its upper end. The spread shows respondents sizing up each arm of the state on its own terms, from the barracks to the government office.

The military's edge holds against every sector outside health and knowledge. Tech entrepreneurs, the best-rated business and finance group, post +6, 10 points short of the armed forces. Lawyers, the highest-scoring professional services group, sit at 0. TV news anchors, the top media role, fall to -3. Clergy/priests, the lone religious group, register -11. Politicians, at -48, trail the armed forces by 64 points. In every one of those sectors, the best entry lands nearer to zero than to the military's mark.

Gallup reports that U.S. adults in its polling voiced more confidence in military veterans than in the military as an institution. The finding hints that views of the armed forces can hinge on whether people picture the organization or the individuals who served in it. Gallup's polling stays within the U.S., so it sheds light on one country's view of its military without speaking for the other countries in the wider survey.

Personal trainers carry a net trust score of +10, which hands the Health and knowledge category four of the five highest spots among the 20 groups surveyed. Doctors, scientists, and teachers claim the other three, and the armed forces stand as the sole group from outside that category to break into the upper tier.

Shared membership hides a steep internal drop. Trainers trail doctors by 33 points and teachers by 27, so they share a label with the most trusted professions without sharing their standing. The armed forces, at +16, sit six points above trainers, a gap less than a fifth of the one separating trainers from doctors.

Trainers build their work around individual attention. Personal fitness trainers assess a client's present fitness level, goals, and skills, then design individualized programs and track how the client progresses. Sessions may involve one client or a small group and can take place at a gym or in a client's home. Certification serves as a common entry requirement before trainers take on clients or coach members of a gym or health club. Employers favor certified candidates, though requirements differ from one facility to the next. Many trainers working in gyms and fitness facilities sell training sessions to members.

Trainers finish above every group in Business and finance, Professional services, Media, Religion, and Politics, along with three of the four Public institutions groups. Their cushion over the nearest of those groups stays slim. They clear tech entrepreneurs by four points and judges and police by five. Their +10 puts them 10 points above lawyers, who rest at zero. At the far end, trainers finish 58 points above politicians, who post the weakest score of the 20 groups. Among the four Health and knowledge groups, trainers post the sole score that falls nearer to zero than to the top mark.

Tech entrepreneurs hold net trust of +6 points, making them the single group in the business and finance category where trust outweighs distrust. Business leaders, bankers, and advertising executives all finish below zero. The nearest of them, business leaders, trails tech entrepreneurs by 14 points.

Adults surveyed across the 31 countries split the corporate world at the break-even mark. Founders of technology companies and the executives who run firms both earn their living in commerce, yet the two groups sit on opposite sides of the line. The ranking's authors flag wide gaps between jobs that share an industry, and business and finance offers a clear case. The business label on its own predicts little about where any one of its jobs will land.

Tech entrepreneurs share their stretch of the scale with public institutions and fitness work. Judges and police each post +5, one point lower, and personal trainers sit four points higher at +10. The sixth-place result leaves tech founders closer to the courts and law enforcement than to any fellow business group.

Their edge over distrust stays narrow. Tech entrepreneurs carry the slimmest margin among the six groups above +5. Doctors, scientists, teachers, the armed forces, and personal trainers all clear a wider gap between confidence and suspicion. Any reader weighing the business world's one positive score should see it as a modest win, far from the broad approval the top of the list enjoys.

Tech founders break a pattern among the groups with positive scores. Every other one comes from either health and knowledge or public institutions. No role in media, professional services, religion, or politics climbs above zero. Lawyers stop at zero without tipping into the plus column. Tech entrepreneurs stand as the one profession to earn net goodwill from outside public service and the health and knowledge fields.

Judges hold net trust of +5 points, a lead over their doubters narrower than that of any group above them on the 20-group list. Tech entrepreneurs, one spot higher, sit a single point ahead at +6. Personal trainers, a fitness occupation, draw a stronger result than the judiciary as well. The three health and knowledge groups at the summit enjoy a level of goodwill the courts do not approach. Judges outscore every media role in the survey, including TV news anchors, the strongest of the three. Respondents who call judges trustworthy outnumber the skeptics, yet the margin leaves the bench closer to the break-even line than to the top of the list.

Judges occupy the middle of the public institutions category, beneath the armed forces and ahead of the civil service. The armed forces, the category's strongest group, sit 11 points above the bench at +16. Government officials and civil servants trail judges by 14 points at -9, which puts them below zero. Three of the four public institutions in the survey hold positive scores, and the administrative arm stands as the lone exception.

Public confidence in the state tips from approval to doubt somewhere between the courtroom and the government office. Uniformed and judicial roles stay in positive territory, while the officials who run day-to-day administration draw more suspicion than faith. The courts sit a long way from political leadership, with government ministers and politicians both among the three lowest scores on the list.

Judges finish five points ahead of lawyers, who break even at 0 in the professional services category. The two legal roles hug the line where trust and distrust cancel out, one a step above it and the other resting on it. Neither commands the broad support the health and knowledge groups receive, and together the two courtroom roles sit nearer neutral ground than firm public backing.

Vocabulary flag: "trust" and "points" recur across paragraphs 1 to 4 of slide 7 as the name and unit of the measure. No precise synonym exists.

Police hold a net trust score of +5 points, the same figure judges post. Respondents placed the two groups on level footing, in back-to-back spots on the list.

Police also mark the final group above zero. Eight of the 20 professions and groups draw more trust than distrust, and police hold the last of those positions. Lawyers come next at 0, which leaves police 5 points clear of an even split between believers and skeptics. A cushion that thin means the doubters nearly match the supporters.

Public institutions show a wide internal spread around police. The armed forces sit 11 points higher at +16, and government officials and civil servants trail police by 14 points at -9. The four bodies stretch across 25 points, and police split the middle of that range with judges. An institutional label alone guarantees no matching regard from respondents.

Police still outscore most of the field. Every media role, the lone religious group, both professional services groups, and both political groups land below them. Three of the four business and finance groups trail as well, with tech entrepreneurs the only exception in that category. Apart from tech entrepreneurs, every group above police comes from the health and knowledge category or the armed forces.

Measured in points, police sit nearer the doctors and scientists at the top than the politicians and ministers at the bottom, even though their position falls near the midpoint of the 20-group list.

Lawyers finish ninth with net trust of 0, which means the respondents who call them trustworthy equal those who call them untrustworthy. No other profession among the 20 lands on that dividing line between trust and distrust.

The neutral result turns lawyers into the hinge of the list. Eight groups above them earn more trust than distrust, and the 11 below them face the reverse. Negative scores outnumber positive ones, so a break-even mark lands in the upper half of the 20.

Lawyers outscore a long roster of groups that hold sway over money, news, faith, and government. Every media role and every business and finance group except tech entrepreneurs falls below them. So do government officials and civil servants, clergy/priests, government ministers, and politicians. Respondents give lawyers a better balance of trust than they give the people who report the news, handle bank accounts, or run for office.

The zero mark sits off-center in the spread of results. Lawyers trail doctors, the top group, by 43 points and finish 48 points clear of politicians at the bottom. Suspicion of the lowest groups runs deeper than faith in the highest ones, and lawyers sit nearer the top as a result.

Judges and police, both at +5, sit in the Public institutions group alongside the armed forces, and all three outscore lawyers. Judges and lawyers share the legal arena, yet judges alone finish with trust ahead of distrust. The 5-point gap between the two courtroom roles is modest, but it divides a positive balance from an even one.

Pollsters, the lone other Professional services group, come in 2 points lower at -2. Neither member of the category climbs above zero, so a draw marks the best result Professional services can claim. Even so, the category outpaces Media, Religion, and Politics, the other three that lack a single positive score.

Pollsters carry a net trust score of -2, the first figure on the 20-group list where distrust edges past trust. Nine groups finish ahead of them and 10 behind, so pollsters open a stretch of 11 groups below zero.

Lawyers, the only other Professional services group, stand two points higher at zero. Neither member of the category lands on the plus side, which puts Professional services alongside Media, Religion, and Politics as categories without a single group in positive territory. Judges and police, the nearest groups with a favorable balance, land seven points above pollsters at +5.

Professional services posts the tightest internal spread of any category with more than one member. Health and knowledge, Public institutions, Business and finance, Media, and Politics all cover wider ranges between their highest and lowest groups. The public's verdict on the field changes little from one role to the other, with lawyers at the break-even mark and pollsters a step beneath it.

Pollsters fare better than every media role. TV news anchors trail them by one point at -3, journalists by eight points at -10, and social media influencers by 42 points at -44. Respondents viewed the people who measure public opinion with less skepticism than any of the three groups in the news and content business, although pollsters themselves land on the negative side.

The -2 score splits the distance between the two ends of the spectrum to within a point, landing 45 points below doctors and 46 points above politicians.

A poll estimates how people feel at one moment in time and makes no attempt to predict what comes next.

Courtney Kennedy of Ipsos suggested that anyone weighing a poll look for a named pollster with credentials and an open account of its methods. Stronger polls, she said, tend to lay out their procedures with greater clarity.

TV news anchors land 11th among the 20 groups with a net trust score of -3, the best result any media role posts in the survey. Distrust outweighs confidence for anchors by a slim margin. The score leaves them three points beneath the break-even mark that lawyers occupy at 0. Anchors are the second of 11 groups to fall below zero. Ten groups stand above them and nine below, which puts anchors one spot past the midpoint of the ranking.

Journalists sit seven points lower at -10, a gap that splits two jobs filed under the same Media category. Skeptics outnumber believers for both roles. The people who deliver the news on television fare better with respondents than journalists as a group do. The seven-point spread between the two roles is more than double the distance separating anchors from the break-even line.

Anchors sit inside a tight cluster of groups near zero. Pollsters score -2, one point above them, and business leaders score -8, five points below. Lawyers, pollsters, and anchors all land within three points of one another. The next step up the list covers a wider distance. Judges and police, both at +5, stand eight points ahead of anchors.

Anchors outpace most of the business world, part of government, and every group in religion and politics. Their -3 beats business leaders, bankers at -10, and advertising executives at -26. Tech entrepreneurs, at +6, form the lone business and finance group ahead of them. Government officials and civil servants trail anchors by six points at -9. Clergy/priests, the survey's only religious group, come in eight points below anchors at -11. Both political groups, government ministers at -37 and politicians at -48, sit deeper in negative territory.

Journalists need 10 points to reach even footing. Within the news business, a three-point shift would lift anchors to neutral ground, less than a third of the climb journalists face.

Business leaders carry a net trust score of -8, which means more of the adults surveyed across 31 countries called them untrustworthy than trustworthy. Their 12th-place finish among the 20 groups puts them in the lower half of the list and makes them the third group with a negative score, after pollsters at -2 and TV news anchors at -3. The figure lands eight points under lawyers, whose score of 0 marks the break-even line.

Tech entrepreneurs, the one business role inside the top 10, outscore business leaders by 14 points. Respondents handed tech entrepreneurs a +6, the lone positive mark in the Business and finance category, and left corporate leadership in negative territory. Two roles from the same sector ended up on opposite sides of the divide between confidence and suspicion.

Business leaders hold second place among the four Business and finance groups. They finish two points ahead of bankers at -10 and 18 points ahead of advertising executives at -26. Their score sits far nearer the bankers' mark than the tech entrepreneurs' result. In the public's view, corporate leadership aligns with finance more than with technology. The four groups average -9.5, and business leaders hover around that midpoint. Outside the category, government officials and civil servants trail them by one point at -9. The near tie puts the people who run companies and the people who staff government offices on the same footing of public doubt.

The score leaves business leaders 51 points below doctors and 40 points above politicians, closer to the bottom of the scale than to the top. Their deficit looks modest beside the deeper hole advertising executives dig at the foot of the category. Three of the four Business and finance roles finish below zero. Distrust is the sector's default, and business leaders share it in a milder form than bankers or advertising executives.

Government officials and civil servants post a net trust score of -9, 28 points above the -37 that government ministers receive. Both roles belong to the machinery of the state, yet respondents drew a sharp line between them. The ranking's authors read the spread as evidence that people separate public administration from political leadership. The table mirrors the split in its own labels, filing civil servants under public institutions and ministers under politics.

Civil servants land 13th of 20, a position that keeps them clear of the political roles clustered near the floor. Business leaders sit one point higher, and journalists one point lower. The administrators rest nine points below the break-even line that lawyers occupy. Among the 11 groups with negative results, only pollsters, TV news anchors, and business leaders fare better. Civil servants occupy the crowded middle of the table, where a handful of points separates one profession from the next.

Civil servants carry the weakest mark among the four public institutions in the survey, and they alone in that category slip below zero. The armed forces reach +16, and judges and police each hold +5. A 25-point gulf separates the military from civil servants. Judges and police, the closest institutional neighbors, keep a clear margin over the civil service. Uniformed and judicial roles stay in positive territory, while the civil service sinks into deficit. No single verdict covers every branch of public service in these results.

Politicians, at -48, trail civil servants by 39 points. Ministers sit closer to politicians than to administrators. Across these three roles, distrust deepens with each step away from public administration and toward political office. Respondents appear to reserve their harshest judgment for the people who hold political power. The staff beneath them receive a measure of leniency, though one that falls short of approval.

Journalists finish with a net trust score of -10, which leaves them tied with bankers and in the middle of the three media roles in the survey. More respondents doubted reporters than believed them, by a margin of 10 percentage points.

The tie links two groups from unrelated fields. Bankers come under business and finance, while journalists belong to media. Adults surveyed across 31 countries handed both the same verdict. Skepticism at this level crosses the boundary between people who handle money and people who handle information.

Reporters occupy the center ground within media, and no role in that category reaches positive territory. TV news anchors stand above them at -3, and social media influencers sink below at -44. Journalists land nearer the anchors than the influencers, which puts them on the less distrusted side of the media field despite their own shortfall.

Journalists fit inside a tight cluster in the lower half of the list. Five groups fall within 3 points of one another: business leaders at -8, government officials and civil servants at -9, journalists and bankers at -10, and clergy/priests at -11. Small differences separate institutions as varied as the civil service, the press, the banks, and the church. The five span four of the ranking's seven categories, from religion to public institutions.

A 14th-place finish puts reporters 53 points below doctors at +43 and 38 points above politicians at -48. Measured by that spread, the press sits closer to the least trusted group than to the most trusted one.

A 15-point gap opens below that cluster, between clergy/priests at -11 and advertising executives at -26. The bottom four groups, from advertising executives to politicians, all register -26 or worse. Reporters face a modest deficit of confidence, and the steep drop-off beneath them separates their standing from the deep distrust facing the lowest groups.

Bankers hold a net trust score of -10, so the share of respondents who call them untrustworthy exceeds the share who call them trustworthy by 10 percentage points. Thirteen groups post a higher score, and five post a lower one. Bankers fall in the lower half of the list, where every group scores below zero.

Bankers occupy the exact center of the business and finance category. Their -10 sits 16 points above the -26 advertising executives record and 16 points below the +6 tech entrepreneurs earn. The banking deficit runs less than half the size of the one advertising executives carry. Business leaders, at -8, finish two points ahead of bankers, and the two groups form a cluster of modest deficits between the sector's lone positive result and its steepest negative one. Three of the four business and finance groups land on the negative side, and bankers come in between the other two.

Bankers sit closer to the bottom of the full list than to its peak. They trail doctors by 53 points and clear politicians by 38. Every health and knowledge group outpaces bankers, as do lawyers at 0 and pollsters at -2. Each public institutions group beats bankers, down to government officials and civil servants, who hold a single-point edge at -9.

Bankers and tech entrepreneurs share a category label yet sit on opposite sides of zero. Adults surveyed across the 31 countries give technology founders a positive verdict and the banking trade a negative one. CNBC reports that analysts pointed to lingering distrust of banks as a main reason financial technology companies grew.

Bankers bear a deficit about one-fifth the size of the one politicians face. Doubt clouds the banking profession, yet it stays far from the depths the bottom three groups reach, each at -37 or worse.

Clergy/priests finish with a net trust score of -11, which leaves the lone religious occupation in the survey on the skeptical side of the ledger at 16th of 20. Doubt prevails over confidence for the people who lead congregations, though by a slimmer margin than the groups trailing them endure.

Religion forms a category with a single entry. Every other group on the list shares its field with at least one peer. Health and knowledge, public institutions, and business and finance each count four members. Media holds three, while professional services and politics each pair two. Clergy/priests stand alone, and the list offers no second faith role to measure them against.

Journalists and bankers each register -10, one point above clergy/priests. Government officials / civil servants at -9 and business leaders at -8 sit a notch higher. Five groups crowd into a three-point band from -8 to -11, covering 12th through 16th place. Pollsters, at -2, and TV news anchors, at -3, hold the milder negative scores above that band. Inside such a tight cluster, the order separating clergy/priests from their neighbors hinges on a point or two.

Advertising executives, at -26, open a 15-point drop beneath clergy/priests. Clergy/priests occupy the last spot above -20 on the list. Four groups sit below that line: advertising executives, government ministers, social media influencers, and politicians. Of the 11 groups under zero, clergy/priests sit seventh, with six gentler scores ahead of them.

Doctors sit 54 points above clergy/priests, and politicians, at -48, fall 37 points beneath the clergy. The armed forces, the highest-scoring group outside health and knowledge, stand 27 points above clergy/priests. Lawyers, at 0, enjoy an 11-point edge over the clergy. Clergy/priests finish 26 points ahead of government ministers and 33 points ahead of social media influencers. They land closer to the bottom group on the list than to the top one.

Advertising executives hold a net trust score of -26 points, the weakest result among the four business and finance groups in the survey. Tech entrepreneurs, the strongest of that quartet at +6, finish 32 points higher. Business leaders at -8 and bankers at -10 also clear the advertising group by wide margins, 18 and 16 points. Bankers, the nearest business peer, sit closer to zero than to advertising executives.

The fall from the middle of the table to this spot is steep. Clergy/priests, one place above at -11, sit 15 points clear of advertising executives. Across the eight groups from lawyers through clergy/priests, scores span a mere 11 points, from 0 to -11. No other pair of neighboring groups below the armed forces sits as far apart as clergy/priests and advertising executives. A single step down from the religious group covers more ground than that entire eight-group middle stretch.

Advertising executives finish 17th of 20, closer to the floor than to the center of the list. Government ministers, the next group down at -37, trail them by 11 points. Politicians, at the bottom with -48, sit 22 points lower. Doctors, at the summit with +43, stand 69 points above advertising executives. Of the 11 groups with negative scores, advertising executives post the fourth-deepest deficit. Every group beneath advertising executives belongs to politics or media, which makes -26 the poorest score for any group outside those two categories.

The business and finance category splits along clear lines. One of its four groups earns a positive score, two hover in the high single digits and low double digits below zero, and advertising executives sit far apart from the rest. Tech entrepreneurs, by contrast, stand closer to the armed forces than to advertising executives. On this scale, respondents treat advertising executives as closer kin to political leadership than to the bankers, business leaders, and tech entrepreneurs who share their category.

Government ministers carry a net trust score of -37 points, the third-worst result among the 20 groups. Doubters outnumber believers by a wide margin, and two groups alone fare worse.

Advertising executives, the next group up the table, score -26. The 11-point slide from that business role to ministers marks the second-largest step between neighboring groups in the bottom half of the list. Only the gap separating clergy/priests from advertising executives runs wider. Every business and finance group, bankers and advertising executives included, earns a milder verdict than the people holding ministerial posts. Business leaders, at -8, stand 29 points ahead of ministers.

Each of the four public institutions in the survey finishes above ministers. The armed forces, judges, and police all hold positive scores, and ministers trail each by more than 40 points. The armed forces, at +16, sit 53 points higher. Judges and police, tied at +5, clear ministers by 42 points.

Politics claims two of the three spots at the foot of the list. Ministers share the category with politicians, who sit 11 points lower at -48. Social media influencers, at -44, land between the two political groups and trail ministers by seven points.

Ministers draw a harsher verdict than every media role except influencers. TV news anchors, the strongest media role at -3, rise 34 points above ministers, and journalists, at -10, sit 27 points clear. Clergy/priests, the lone religious group, hold a 26-point edge at -11.

Ministers sit 37 points below lawyers, whose score of zero marks the line where trust and distrust balance. Pollsters, one notch below that line at -2, outscore ministers by 35 points. The distance to doctors at the opposite end stretches to 80 points.

No other category in the table keeps every member below -30, so politics stands as the one field where skepticism reaches each role it contains.

Social media influencers post a net trust score of -44, the second-weakest result among the 20 professions and the poorest for any group outside politics. Only politicians land beneath them. Government ministers, the other political group near the bottom, finish 7 points higher at -37.

Influencers trail the other two media roles by a wide margin. TV news anchors score -3 and journalists -10, which leaves influencers 41 points behind anchors and 34 behind journalists. Visual Capitalist reads this spread as a sign of a major divide in how people view different media roles.

No other grouping in the survey stretches as far from its best member to its worst. Media jobs land at 11th, 14th, and 19th in the 20-group list. The government split between civil servants and ministers, the other sharp gap the source flags inside government, covers less ground than the distance separating anchors from influencers. Averaging the three roles into one media figure would mask the rift, landing at a number that describes none of them.

The influencer deficit runs more than four times as deep as the journalists' and more than 14 times as deep as the anchors'. Distrust outweighs trust for all three media roles, yet the shortfall for the two news jobs looks modest beside the hole influencers face. Anchors and journalists hover within reach of the break-even mark. Influencers, by contrast, sit within sight of the scale's floor.

Advertising executives, at -26 the lowest business and finance score, finish 18 points clear of influencers. Clergy/priests at -11 and bankers at -10 sit more than 30 points above them. Doctors, at +43, hold an 87-point edge. Every business group, every public institution, and the lone religious role outscore influencers.

Respondents place influencers nearer to politicians and ministers than to the anchors and journalists who share their field.

Politicians finish with a net score of -48 points, the weakest of all 20 groups, after 13% of respondents called them trustworthy against 61% who called them untrustworthy.

Skeptics outnumber believers by close to five to one. Each respondent who vouched for politicians stood alongside about 4.7 who dismissed them. The 61% figure also forms an outright majority, so more than half of everyone surveyed put politicians in the untrustworthy column. Politicians are the only group whose separate trustworthy and untrustworthy shares appear in the published results. Their -48 is the one score on the list readers can break into its two parts.

The two shares account for 74% of respondents. The other 26% landed in neither camp and offered no verdict either way. Those uncommitted respondents form the only pool politicians could win over without changing anyone's mind.

Politics posts the poorest average of the seven categories, at -42.5 across its two groups. Media comes next at -19 for its three roles, leaving the political category 23.5 points behind the second-worst field. Social media influencers account for most of that media deficit, pulling the category below the scores of TV news anchors and journalists, two roles that sit far closer to neutral. Politics has no such buffer. Its other group, government ministers, also draws heavy distrust. Influencers, at -44, still sit four points above politicians and form the politicians' closest neighbor on the list.

Politicians would remain in negative territory if every one of the uncommitted 26% swung to their side. Their trustworthy share would climb to 39%, leaving them 22 points shy of the 61% who distrust them. An even score would require 24% of respondents to cross from distrust to trust, leaving both shares at 37%. Any path to a positive score runs through people who have written politicians off.

#5406. A cruise ship sold as a forever home left 203 residents in Cambodia as Iran war fuel costs hit up to $8,000 a cabin

The Villa Vie Odyssey, a cruise ship advertised as a forever home for more than 200 residents, sailed out of Sihanoukville, Cambodia, on Wednesday with only crew aboard. Its lender has taken possession of the vessel and is now paying for the crew, fuel, and upkeep.

Florida-based Villa Vie Residences says fuel did it in. The company said its monthly fuel cost per cabin climbed from $1,800 to between $6,000 and $8,000 after the Iran war sent oil prices soaring, and that passing the full increase on to residents was not realistic. It sold years of life at sea at a set price, and its highest variable cost more than tripled.

A Cambodian official put the count at 203 passengers and 156 crew, and most residents were American. The ship is reportedly bound for Singapore, where it could eventually be auctioned.

Before it landed on the chopping block, the 642-foot Odyssey was home to people who planned to stay for years. Mechanical problems kept it in Belfast, Northern Ireland, until October 2024, when it finally set off on a voyage meant to circle the globe every three and a half years, reaching 147 countries on the first loop. A four-year stay cost $319,998 for two people sharing a cabin.

For others, it was a lifetime commitment. Some sold their houses, and the company’s Endless Horizons program charged a one-time $299,999 for a single cabin or $499,999 for a double. When Fortune covered the launch in 2023, Villa Vie was selling cabins from $99,000, plus annual fees of $21,000 to $48,000.

As recently as July, the company announced a second ship, Legacy, saying Odyssey had sold 85% of its residences. Then on Oct. 27, residents were told they had roughly eight hours to leave. The ship was 754 days into its planned voyage.

“Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port,” the company said in a statement the week it halted operations. It wasn’t enough.

Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin, both 56, were longtime Maui residents swept up in the idea of seeing the world from a residential cruise ship. What surprised them most was how much cheaper life at sea could be: no car or mortgage payments, meals included, laundry handled. It was the deal of a lifetime.

In their final vlog from the ship, the couple said they started hearing about the company’s financial trouble two months before they were told to leave. The waiting made the dream “emotionally exhausting.”

“I felt really drained the last two months … you get beat down, and then the next day or two, like: oh boy, we have hope, we have investors, we have this coming, and then the next two days, you get beat down again,” Bodin said.

The couple says they are not in dire financial straits and plan to keep traveling through Southeast Asia. But they know residents who put their life savings and retirement funds into the ship and now don’t know what comes next.

Founder and executive chairman Mikael Petterson has taken responsibility, calling himself “the villain in the story” in an interview with Business Insider. He still maintains the Iran war is what sank the business.

“I think we would have been absolutely fine and we would have seen this through, if there was no Iran war,” Petterson said.

Before U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran began on Feb. 28, Brent crude traded around $70 a barrel. It has since repeatedly broken $100, topping $126 this spring. Crude has slipped back below $100, but regular gasoline still averaged $4.10 a gallon on Nov. 4, according to AAA.

U.S. consumers paid $160 billion more for gasoline and diesel from March 1 through Oct. 14 than they would have without the war, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. That is the largest bill of any country, Fortune reported.

Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, estimated in mid-October that the war has cost the average American household nearly $2,000. About $1,100 of that comes from higher energy prices. The rest comes from higher interest rates and the cost of military operations.

For Villa Vie, the next deadline is its own. The company has given itself about 60 days to restructure and raise new money, says no outcome is assured, and Petterson has told NBC News that a Chapter 11 filing may be necessary.

#5405. Starfish Space loses contact with its Otter spacecraft, ending satellite inspection mission

by Alan Boyle on Nov 3, 2026 at 10:50 pmNovember 3, 2026 at 11:10 pm

Starfish Space says it can no longer receive data from its first full-scale Otter space vehicle, bringing a $15 million NASA mission to inspect inoperable satellites to a premature end.

In a LinkedIn post, the Tukwila, Wash.-based startup said its Otter 24C spacecraft was not able to complete all the objectives for the mission, known as Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability (SSPICY). “Starfish and NASA are exploring opportunities to fulfill mission objectives through other Starfish missions,” the company said.

The Otter spacecraft was sent into low Earth orbit aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket on Oct. 1. “Following a successful launch and deployment, Starfish established two-way contact with the spacecraft and successfully commanded Otter 24C, downlinking significant telemetry during early operations,” Starfish said.

However, the mission team lost contact with the oven-sized spacecraft during the commissioning process. “An investigation into the loss of communications has determined that fault protection on the satellite bus provided by Astro Digital had an error that turned off the radio and prevented re-establishing communications,” the company said.

Starfish, NASA and Astro Digital determined that the spacecraft was unrecoverable.

In today’s update, Starfish said it is working closely with Astro Digital to fix the fault protection system and update testing procedures for future Otters.

“Developing new capabilities in space requires taking on difficult challenges, learning quickly and applying those lessons to what comes next,” Starfish said. “The work completed through Otter 24C will directly contribute to the success of future Otter missions as Starfish continues developing the technologies and operations required to make satellite servicing a routine capability in orbit.”

Greg Stover, director of the Advanced Research and Technology Division at NASA Headquarters, said in a news release that “commercial capabilities like Starfish’s are critical for a competitive U.S. space economy and strong American leadership in low Earth orbit.”

“Technology demonstrations allow us to quickly test new systems, learn from their performance, and iterate so that we are pushing the boundaries of what’s possible with every mission,” Stover said. “NASA will continue taking on bold challenges in close collaboration with our industry partners.”

Several other Otter missions remain on tap — including a satellite disposal job for the Pentagon’s Space Development Agency, two commercial satellite servicing missions in geostationary Earth orbit, and two servicing missions for the U.S. Space Force.

Starfish Space is also continuing to test an Otter Pup prototype that was launched into orbit last year. Last week, it posted a video to LinkedIn showing a close approach to a target satellite known as ElaraSat. The company says it is preparing for a docking attempt “and a chance to make history.”

#5404. AI agents went shopping for TVs and laptops—and messed up nearly 50% of the time, study shows

As personal AI agents like Muse or Claude become part of daily life, more people are asking them to carry out shopping tasks. But there’s a problem: the agents aren’t very good at shopping. In a first-of-its-kind study, Visa instructed 22 different agents to purchase three everyday items—a TV, a laptop and a hair appliance—and, while some agents did significantly better than others, the overall success rate was only around 57%.

The results of the study are available on a new website by Visa that shows the outcome of 15 separate shopping expeditions by each of the 22 agents. Unsurprisingly, the agents powered by more cutting edge AI models fared best, with the Aragon 4 version of Google’s Gemini and the Wonder version of Meta’s Making notching the highest scores. Both agents made a successful purchase 82% of the time. A Claude agent came in third with a 76% success rate, while an OpenAI agent finished 6th with a 64% success rate.

The diagram below from Visa shows the performance of all 22 models. The vertical axis scores the agents’ success rate, while the horizontal one reflects the cost to run each shopping inquiry. (Visa notes that the five most expensive models succeeded on average 67% of the time, while the cheapest five scored 50%).

The agents’ struggle to make a successful purchase is rooted in part in a simple reality: The motivations behind any given purchase are often complicated and, in many cases, consumers lack information and are not certain what they want.

Visa’s experiment sought to capture this reality by, in the case of TV shoppers, assigning a list of attributes they needed in a television—for instance, compatibility with a child’s gaming console, a 30-day return window, and a model with Dolby Vision. As is the case with real world consumers, the purchaser (who in this case was also an agent) would volunteer some information, but not all of it.

The upshot is that, for an AI agent to succeed in Visa’s experiment, it had to interact with the shopper in a way that would elicit the missing information in a reasonable time. Success amounted to buying a TV that matched the shopper’s needs but, in many cases, the agents bought the wrong product, or simply failed to suggest something suitable at all.

“We’re not there yet from a trust or technology perspective. But we’ll soon get into a world where consumers can trust and delegate,” Visa’s Global Head of Growth, Rubail Birwadker, told Fortune.

Birwadker noted that agent-driven shopping is still in its early days, but that it is advancing rapidly. He added that the focus of Visa’s experiment—product discovery—is just one element of this new type of commerce that retailers and AI companies are trying to figure out.

For AI agents to enter the shopping mainstream, companies will also have to sort out smooth and secure payments—a challenge that Visa and its rival Mastercard are already seeking to address by educating merchants and building tools to facilitate so-called agentic commerce.

There are also new and unresolved legal issues when it comes to AI agents going shopping. Most notably, it’s still unclear who should bear the liability when agents make rogue purchases or commit fraud.

According to Birwadker, these questions will get resolved over time in the same way that an earlier generation of consumers and merchants learned to use ecommerce—he added, though, that agent-based shopping is going to be a very different experience than how we shop online today.

In announcing the results of its agent shopping experiment, Visa also rolled out a website that allows consumers to interact with the agents used in its survey.

Jeff John Roberts is the Finance and Crypto editor at Fortune, overseeing coverage of the blockchain and how technology is changing finance.

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:07 am

Seattle-based pet care marketplace Rover is adding two executives to its leadership team: former Motus CFO Vik Rajagopal as chief financial officer and Textio co-founder Jensen Harris as president of marketplace, product and technology.

Rajagopal succeeds Charlie Wickers, who served as Rover’s CFO from 2022 to 2025. Harris succeeds Brent Turner, who was Rover’s president and chief operating officer before he was named CEO last year.

Rajagopal spent nearly a decade at Amazon, starting in 2011 as a finance lead for Amazon Global Selling, the program that helps sellers reach customers in other countries. He later became a general manager in Amazon’s retail business, running the U.S. shoes and luggage stores and the home store, as well as Amazon’s U.S. Vendor Success Program.

He left Amazon in late 2020 to become CFO of Logos, a maker of Bible study software backed by private equity firm Cove Hill Partners. He was promoted to CEO about a year later, replacing the company’s founder, and led Logos until April 2024. He was most recently CFO at Motus, which makes software that companies use to manage and reimburse employees who drive for work.

Earlier in his career, Rajagopal was an investment banker at Wells Fargo Securities and worked in corporate development at Symantec. He holds a bachelor’s degree from Yale and an MBA from Northwestern’s Kellogg School of Management.

“Rover is a Seattle company that was built the right way from day one — solving a real customer pain point with a strong product, solid economics, and a culture that is poised for long-term success,” Rajagopal said in a news release on Wednesday.

Harris co-founded Seattle-based Textio in 2014 with Kieran Snyder, his wife, after both worked on productivity software at Microsoft. The startup used AI to analyze workplace writing such as job posts and performance reviews. Harris was Textio’s CTO for nearly eight years, then chief experience officer, before taking over as CEO from Snyder in January 2024. He handed the CEO role to Colleen Gallagher in January 2026 and remains with Textio as founder emeritus.

Textio has raised $42.5 million from investors and went through rounds of layoffs in 2024 and 2025 under Harris. As CEO, he led the launch of Lavalier, an AI-based interview intelligence platform.

Before Textio, Harris spent more than 15 years at Microsoft, where he led the redesign of the Office user interface that produced the Ribbon, and later led user experience for Windows and the touch interface for the original Surface.

After leaving the CEO role at Textio, Harris founded Expedition 60, a firm that helps companies rework how they build software with AI.

“Our pets give us unconditional love, and they deserve the very best in return,” Harris said in a statement, adding that he shares a home with “three very opinionated cats.”

Rover was born at a 2011 Seattle Startup Weekend event, where venture capitalist Greg Gottesman pitched the idea. Aaron Easterly led the company as CEO for 14 years, taking it through the pandemic, a public offering and a $2.3 billion take-private deal with Blackstone in 2024. He stepped down last year and became executive chair, handing the CEO role to Turner.

Rover now operates in 18 countries across North America, Europe and Australia, and says sitters and walkers on its platform have provided 50 million bookings to date. Its brands include cat-sitting marketplaces Meowtel and Cat in a Flat, and Australia-based Mad Paws. Beyond sitting and walking, Rover now offers training in the U.S. and is testing other services.

#5402. Everyone is Using AI Now. Here’s What Sets the Companies Using It Well Apart.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI adoption has become almost meaningless as a measure of competitive advantage.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

AI adoption has become almost meaningless as a measure of competitive advantage. Nearly every company now has access to similar models, tools and capabilities. That’s why the conversation needs to shift from AI adoption to AI outcomes. This means using AI to fundamentally change how you serve customers, develop products, make decisions, generate demand or operate your business. It includes improving the economics of the business, accelerating processes or producing a level of quality that wasn’t possible before.

The companies that will stand out will have figured out where AI can create a meaningful business advantage and have redesigned their processes around it.

Companies can easily fall into the trap of only focusing on making existing work slightly faster. And that’s problematic. We see this frequently in marketing and communications. Companies take an existing process like writing content, creating reports, researching prospects and developing campaigns and then use AI to make each individual step faster. That can certainly improve productivity, but it doesn’t necessarily change the underlying economics or effectiveness of the work.

For example, if AI produces a press release that communicates essentially the same message as a human-written version, the primary impact is on drafting efficiency. Reach, audience engagement and the level of interest generated are separate factors that determine the release’s overall business impact.

The bigger opportunity is to ask whether AI allows you to rethink the process entirely. Can you identify market signals earlier? Can you develop and test more differentiated messaging? Can you personalize communications at a scale that wasn’t practical before? Can you understand what customers, prospects, journalists or even AI-driven discovery systems are responding to?

The danger of focusing only on speed is that companies end up doing more of the same work, faster, rather than looking at whether they should be doing the work differently in the first place.

I’m encouraged by successful examples of companies using AI in the right way. The strongest ones tend to involve companies using AI to augment human decision-making rather than simply to automate human tasks.

In communications, for example, AI can help teams process and synthesize enormous amounts of information like research, competitor activity, market conversations, customer feedback, media coverage and emerging topics much faster than a human team could do manually.

Someone said in a meeting recently, after we’d used AI to review some survey responses, that what took us a few minutes would normally have required a room full of people working for days. The value comes when experienced professionals use those insights to make better strategic decisions about positioning, messaging, audiences and timing.

Another strong use case is using AI to detect patterns that would otherwise be difficult to see. Instead of asking AI to produce more content, companies can use it to determine which topics matter to their audiences, where their narrative is gaining traction, where there are gaps and what questions customers are actually asking. That combination is where I see some of the greatest potential: AI for scale and pattern recognition, humans for judgment and context.

At Force4, we’re thinking about AI as a fundamental change in how communications work rather than simply another productivity tool. For example, we’re increasingly looking at how companies are identified not only through traditional search and media but through AI-driven discovery. That changes the communications challenge. It’s no longer enough to create content that ranks or gets published. Companies need to build the credibility, clearness and body of information that enables AI systems to accurately understand and surface them.

We’re using AI to help us analyze information, discover patterns, accelerate research and develop communications more efficiently. But the strategic decisions still require human insight like what a company should stand for, which audiences matter most, what stories are worth telling and how those stories connect to business objectives.

That’s an important distinction for us. We don’t view AI as replacing the expertise of our team. We view it as strengthening what our team can see, understand and accomplish.

I recommend using these five questions to evaluate your use of AI in terms of whether it will genuinely change the economics/speed/quality of their business:

What business problem are we trying to solve? Don’t start with the technology. Start with the business outcome. If the answer is simply “We need to use more AI,” try again.

Does AI materially change the economics? Can you reduce a cost, increase revenue, expand capacity or do something that previously required substantially more resources?

Does it materially improve speed? Not just shaving minutes off a task but accelerating an important business process such as getting a product to market, responding to customers or identifying an opportunity.

Does it improve quality or enable something that wasn’t previously possible? This may ultimately be the most important question. If AI only produces the same result faster, the advantage may be temporary. If it produces a fundamentally better result or enables new capabilities, that is much more strategically important.

What still requires human judgment? The best implementations are thoughtful about where humans add the most value.

AI can process information and observe patterns at extraordinary scale, but context, judgment, creativity, accountability and understanding the nuances of a business still matter enormously. Stop measuring AI success by how many tools they have deployed or how many employees are using them. Measure what has actually changed.

If AI hasn’t changed the economics, speed or quality of an important part of the business, you may have improved productivity, but you probably haven’t created a competitive advantage yet. The real opportunity is to identify areas where AI can fundamentally change how the business works and redesign those processes around the technology rather than simply adding AI to what you already do.

AI adoption has become almost meaningless as a measure of competitive advantage. Nearly every company now has access to similar models, tools and capabilities. That’s why the conversation needs to shift from AI adoption to AI outcomes. This means using AI to fundamentally change how you serve customers, develop products, make decisions, generate demand or operate your business. It includes improving the economics of the business, accelerating processes or producing a level of quality that wasn’t possible before.

The companies that will stand out will have figured out where AI can create a meaningful business advantage and have redesigned their processes around it.

Companies can easily fall into the trap of only focusing on making existing work slightly faster. And that’s problematic. We see this frequently in marketing and communications. Companies take an existing process like writing content, creating reports, researching prospects and developing campaigns and then use AI to make each individual step faster. That can certainly improve productivity, but it doesn’t necessarily change the underlying economics or effectiveness of the work.

#5401. Apple and Home Depot join list of objectors to tokenized stock plan pushed by NYSE owner

An ambitious joint venture  to bring U.S. stocks onto the blockchain appears to be on life support. The venture, cochaired by former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo, and led by crypto firm OKX and the parent company of the New York Stock Exchange, announced plans last month to offer round-the-clock trading of tokenized shares of 62 public companies. But as of Thursday, 54 of those companies had objected to having their shares traded on the platform.

Aerospace manufacturer Boeing and business software maker ServiceNow joined the objection list on Wednesday, a day after Apple, Home Depot and GE Vernova filed objections. Earlier objectors include some of corporate America’s biggest names, from Microsoft, Alphabet, and Nvidia to JPMorgan Chase and Walmart.

Home Depot declined to comment. Boeing, ServiceNow, Apple, and GE Vernova did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

Companies outside OKXICE’s original proposed lineup have also filed objections, including Wells Fargo, Nebius Group, Arm Holdings, Cerebras Systems, and Cigna Group.

The expanded objection list comes a month after Cuomo announced the tokenized stock trading venue in a social media post. The venture was born out of a temporary exemption granted by the Securities and Exchange Commission in September that allows qualifying platforms to offer trading in tokenized stocks without registering as national securities exchanges, provided they meet certain conditions.

The eight companies in OKXICE’s original proposed lineup without a disclosed objection so far predominantly have ties to crypto or blockchain. They include USDC issuer Circle Internet Group, crypto exchange Coinbase, trading platform Robinhood, digital asset custodian BitGo, bitcoin treasury company Strategy and tokenization company Securitize. Software company Palantir and server maker Super Micro Computer round out the list.

OKXICE declined to say whether the growing number of objections would affect its planned launch.

The SEC approved the exemption two days after the Clarity Act, a bill to establish a regulatory framework for digital assets, stalled in the Senate. Under the exemption, platforms like OKXICE do not need a company’s permission to offer trading in tokenized versions of its shares. Instead, they must notify the company and give it 30 days from receipt to object and block the listing, as Fortune reported earlier.

Applied Optoelectronics, a networking equipment maker among the companies to file objections, previously told Fortune that the new framework’s potential impact on its stock’s pricing, liquidity and volatility remained unclear. The company also expressed concern that investors might mistakenly believe it sponsored or endorsed the offering.

“At this stage, we don’t see a clear benefit to AOI or our shareholders that justifies these uncertainties,” a spokesperson said.

#5400. I Returned as CEO Just as AI Took Off. These 4 Lessons Kept My Spending Honest

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Here’s what I’ve learned about striking the right balance between fiscal responsibility and creating real value with AI.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I picked an interesting time to return to my company as CEO.

I came back in early 2024 with a mission: rebuild our tech business around profitable growth. That shift was part of a broader trend in which companies from Netflix to Meta to Peloton shifted focus from growth and revenue at any cost to profitability.

My return, after stepping back for two years, also coincided with the rapid rise of large language models. The business world had changed during my absence, and it was changing faster every day.

I’d founded the company in 2005, so I was no stranger to tech upheavals. I knew that AI would have to play a central role in our transformation. But I also saw a disconnect. Too many companies were throwing money at AI, with little apparent regard for the bottom line.

We had to invest. But we needed discipline. How could I stay fiscally responsible, lead the business to profitability and make sure AI created real value for our customers and us?

Here’s what I’ve learned about finding the right balance.

Few companies have pockets as deep as the Magnificent 7, which can absorb a failed AI bet. If you don’t, every investment must be targeted and financially defensible.

When I returned, we were approaching a billion dollars in revenue but with limited adjusted EBITDA. That shaped the agenda for everything that followed, including our AI spending. A year after I came back, we set a goal: $100 million in free cash flow within three years, proof of the business’s underlying value and durability.

It all started with finding cost savings. This bought us time to conduct a full operating review, see the full investment picture and focus our resources rather than funding every AI initiative.

Financially defensible means holding each AI commitment to the same bar as our free cash flow target. If a bet doesn’t clearly protect or advance that number, it doesn’t get funded, no matter how promising the technology looks.

That bar is easiest to miss on the cost side, where multiyear contracts for coding tools like Codex, Cursor and Claude can lock a company into tens of millions in spending. And unlike, say, personal computers or many cloud services, AI doesn’t necessarily get cheaper as the technology matures. Larger, more powerful models can cost much more to run.

Just ask Uber, which burned through its entire budget for AI coding tools in just four months, leaving its COO questioning whether the return justified the cost. At our scale, where every million matters to adjusted EBITDA and free cash flow, a move like that could erase the progress we need to show shareholders.

The solution: match the AI model — and its cost — to the task. We chose OpenCode, an open-source, model-agnostic coding tool, over locked-in frontier subscriptions. This lets us switch to cost-effective LLMs for relatively simple tasks, like crunching retail data.

Stepping back into the CEO role also meant determining how big a threat AI posed to our business. Almost overnight, the market had decided that every SaaS company was potentially under threat.

By early this year, software companies faced growing pressure to rebuild their pricing models around AI consumption. Spoiler alert: we didn’t go that route. Instead of racing to adopt a new strategy, we considered where AI fit naturally into our existing one.

FOMO can be an expensive way to make business decisions. For example, a third of US hiring managers who cut a role because of AI have since rehired for that job or a similar one. That pattern extends well beyond hiring to any AI-related investment made in haste.

Companies need a sense of urgency in the AI era, but it has to serve the strategy, not replace it. Before following a trend, ask two questions: Does it move the business in the direction you’ve already chosen? And can you explain how it will create measurable value?

Wondering why we didn’t rebuild our pricing around tokens? Our business model already aligned our incentives with customer success.

Most of our revenue comes from transaction fees, which grow when our customers’ businesses grow. Switching to AI-usage pricing would have weakened that alignment by tying revenue to how much technology customers consume, rather than how much value they gain from it.

If your business model rewards results, that’s worth defending rather than abandoning it for the latest pricing fad.

The more important question is what customers actually need AI to do. For example, the people who use our products wear many hats: marketer, social media manager, inventory manager, analyst, in-store experience expert — sometimes all in the same day. AI can help them juggle those responsibilities by doing everything from delivering data-backed insights to recommending new brands to quickly building a professional website.

Because our success depends on merchants’ success, our starting question was how AI could make their lives easier, not how much they might use it.

Before deploying AI for customers, figure out where they struggle. Technology will keep changing, but the fundamentals of delivering real value won’t.

I came back to a tangled web. We had two flagship products, a host of different systems from acquisitions and data spread across dozens of pockets in the company. A lot of that work still ran on Google Sheets, and I doubt we were alone there.

AI is a golden opportunity to streamline how a business works, but only if you don’t confuse adoption with outcomes. Simply having access to the technology won’t make a company more productive on its own.

That distinction is critical. Only about 10% of S&P 500 companies had deeply integrated AI into their business processes as of 2025, while roughly the same share were using it directly to produce goods or deliver services.

The real gains come from combining proprietary data with redesigned workflows. We used AI to connect data sources that had been siloed for years and build a new approach to revenue operations. Instead of asking team members to hunt across systems and scour spreadsheets, we could bring the right information together in one place.

That work reinforced something important: the internal sprawl we were fixing probably resembled what our customers face, often with far fewer resources to solve it.

So the AI systems we build for ourselves can become a proving ground for the products we create for merchants. When a solution helps our teams make sense of scattered data, there’s a good chance it can help our customers do the same.

Ultimately, putting the customer first is what it’s all about for any business in the AI era. Almost two years into our rebuild, I know rapid technological change will bring many more surprises. By staying disciplined and focused on customer needs, we’ll be ready for whatever’s next.

I picked an interesting time to return to my company as CEO.

I came back in early 2024 with a mission: rebuild our tech business around profitable growth. That shift was part of a broader trend in which companies from Netflix to Meta to Peloton shifted focus from growth and revenue at any cost to profitability.

My return, after stepping back for two years, also coincided with the rapid rise of large language models. The business world had changed during my absence, and it was changing faster every day.

#5399. Finpilot raises $10M for AI agents that handle the grunt work for institutional investors

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:04 am

Seattle startup Finpilot, which uses AI agents to take the paperwork off the plates of people who invest money for hospitals, pension funds and foundations, has raised $10 million in a Series A round.

The round was led by Bay Area venture firm Lobby Capital, with participation from Madrona, which led Finpilot’s $4 million seed round in 2024. Finpilot, which has raised about $14.5 million since its 2023 founding, plans to use the new funding to expand its product and hire across the company.

Its customers include in-house investment teams at institutions and firms that manage money on their behalf. In the industry, they’re known as allocators, because they spread capital across outside fund managers. Much of their information arrives from fund managers as PDFs and spreadsheets, and someone has to read the reports, pull out the numbers and enter them into the right systems.

Finpilot pulls that information into one place and has its agents handle much of the work. The idea is to let investment teams spend their time on judgment and decisions, not on reading data from documents and typing it into a database, said Lakshay Chauhan, Finpilot’s co-founder and CEO, in an interview.

“Nobody wakes up like, ‘All right, I’m excited to do that,'” he said.

It’s a change of course for the company. When GeekWire covered its seed round, Finpilot was building a ChatGPT-style tool for analysts researching public companies. It shifted to allocators in mid-2024, Chauhan said, after concluding that AI added only marginal value in public markets, where Bloomberg and S&P Capital IQ had already organized most of the data.

“There’s no Bloomberg for what they do,” he said of allocators.

Customers include Seattle Children’s, Children’s Health in Dallas, Hackensack Meridian Health in New Jersey, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Wyoming, the Wyoming Retirement System, outsourced investment firm TIFF, and Seattle wealth management firm Laird Norton Wetherby. Some of those institutions hadn’t changed their core systems in 15 years, Chauhan said.

Finpilot has about 28 institutional customers in all, and revenue has grown tenfold since the start of the year, he said. It hasn’t lost a customer yet, he noted.

How it works: Finpilot pulls an institution’s data from its portfolio management system, document storage and other sources into a single record, matching each fund, holding and client to one identifier. Users ask questions in a chat window and set up agents to handle recurring work.

In an example Chauhan described, an agent could review updates from 35 private equity managers at the end of a quarter, figure out what changed and point an analyst to the three things that need attention. Agents also prepare briefings before meetings with fund managers, and they ask a person for approval when a step needs one.

Some customers run Finpilot alongside their existing software. Others have used it to replace older customer relationship management and research management systems, where investment teams log their dealings with fund managers.

Chauhan said Finpilot most often gets compared with general-purpose AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, including finance-focused versions like Claude for Financial Services, and with legacy CRM vendors.

Chauhan said the difference is accuracy. A 10-page report from a chatbot has to be checked number by number before it goes to a chief investment officer. In Finpilot, every number links back to the document it came from, so it can be checked.

In finance, he said, “you cannot be wrong.”

Finpilot runs its own in-house model for the high-volume job of reading financial documents, and uses models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google for other tasks. It doesn’t train AI models on customer data and keeps each customer’s data separate, Chauhan said.

Founders: Chauhan grew up in India and came to the U.S. for a master’s degree in aerospace engineering. He interned at Boeing in Seattle, but when he graduated, he said, many full-time aerospace jobs required U.S. citizenship or permanent residency, and he was in the country on a visa.

He went to work for an engineering optimization software company and studied quantitative investing on the side. That led him to a paper by John Alberg, co-founder of Seattle investment firm Euclidean Technologies, which uses machine learning to pick stocks. Chauhan called Alberg repeatedly to propose working together, and Alberg eventually hired him. Chauhan later led AI at Euclidean.

Alberg is Finpilot’s co-founder and executive chairman but isn’t involved in day-to-day operations. His late father, Tom Alberg, co-founded Madrona.

Finpilot has about 14 employees, up from four in 2024. All are based in Seattle except one in Boise, Idaho. The company recently moved into the AGC Building on Lake Union after outgrowing its old office.

What’s next: Finpilot plans to fill six or seven jobs in the next few months, in product, marketing, client success, sales and business development, and about as many early next year.

Part of the money will go to implementation teams, Chauhan said. Their job is to sit down with each customer, learn how its investment team works and show it how to redo that work with AI agents.
