#5398. OpenAI’s Dots are coming up against the price of privacy, and the price of compute

Welcome to Eye on AI. Beatrice Nolan here. In today’s issue:

OpenAI took its Dev Day roadshow to London this week, attempting to sell the city’s developers on Dots, the company’s new, always-on AI assistant.

The company first announced Dots at its big annual developer event in San Francisco a month ago, pitching them as its flagship agentic offering. Whereas tools like Codex, the company’s coding assistant, wait for a user’s instructions, Dots are meant to be proactive. The assistant learns a user’s goals, watches their inbox and work tools, and starts tasks before they ask. (Dots aren’t available in Europe yet, but OpenAI said it is working with European regulators to change that.)

The industry is betting that proactive personal agents are the natural next step for AI, potentially driving as much value on the consumer side as coding agents did on the enterprise side. It’s an increasingly urgent new market for the industry right now, as companies, including Apple and Goldman Sachs, move to cap some employees’ AI spend, a trend that could dent revenue growth at the leading AI labs.

Given the stakes, it’s not surprising that OpenAI is arriving in a crowded market. Meta’s Muse got there first and has proved hugely popular with consumers; Elon Musk’s xAI has Grok Bot; and Anthropic has its own Duet on the market too.

How is OpenAI positioning Dots against that competition? By betting on high-end, high-spend users first.

“There are many other assistants out there, some of which have great UI interfaces, but what they can accomplish can be less advanced,” Romain Huet, OpenAI’s head of developer experience, told me. “We really wanted to nail the enterprise and pro use case first, because I think that’s where people will see the most value.”

That strategy also reflects how expensive these agents are to run. As my colleague Emily Forlini reported this week, Musk has said Grok Bot’s running costs are “unsustainably high relative to revenue,” and Adam Fry, who runs ChatGPT’s consumer business, told reporters that Dots are “on the compute-heavy side.” OpenAI is trying to combat this by routing some Dot tasks to Terra, a smaller GPT-6.1 model, instead of sending them all to the larger GPT-6 Astra, Emily wrote.

Huet told me OpenAI is aiming for token efficiency to keep costs down. He said the company’s Terra model can perform better than Astra in some areas, such as computer use and writing, at “a tenth of the price.” The company wants “the most amount of value delivered per dollar invested in these Dots,” he said.

These always-on agents also raise issues around consent, Whittaker points out. The people who email or message a personal assistant user, she argues, never agreed to have an AI read and ingest what they send.

“Muse is logging people’s contact lists, the people they talk to,” Whittaker said at the Masters of Scale Summit in October. “If you install Muse, and I am in your contact list, Muse now has my information. They are logging when we talk to each other…That could be extraordinarily serious for somebody working on human rights in an authoritarian country who is trying to communicate data with somebody outside of that country.”

“I personally said to my dot: I would love for you to categorize my email all the time. I would like for you to prep, possibly, what my answer might be, but don’t send any emails on my behalf ever, and don’t send any Slack messages on my behalf ever,” he said. “I want to do that myself.”

Ok, before we get to the rest of the AI news, I want to mention the amazing line up of speakers at our upcoming Fortune Brainstorm AI conference in San Francisco, which is taking place on Dec. 7 and 8. Come hear about the latest in AI from OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora, AI luminaries Fei-Fei Li and Andrew Ng, and LinkedIn cofounder and Greylock partner Reid Hoffman—and that’s just to name a few of the many incredible builders, doers, and thinkers who will be on hand. I’ll be there, of course, alongside my Fortune AI reporting colleagues Jeremy Kahn and Emily Forlini. Why not join us? You can apply to attend here. And with that, here’s the rest of the AI news.

The pledges are part of a new framework that OpenAI wants lawmakers to turn into binding rules for AI infrastructure. Under the plan, the company says it will pay the full cost of the power it uses, plus the grid upgrades utilities need to serve its sites. It will also publish water and electricity use for each facility, ask communities for input before construction, and favor low-water cooling. The move comes as opposition to data centers has hardened across the U.S. In this week’s midterms, voters backed restrictions on development in dozens of local ballot measures. OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, said the framework would help set “a very high floor” for how the industry moves forward. The company said it had been working on the changes for months. Read more in Bloomberg.

Wu led product for Claude Code and later also took on Anthropic’s Cowork product. She left the company at the end of October, and this week she announced she will lead product management for OpenAI’s Core Products team. She will report to Thibault Sottiaux, who has led work on OpenAI’s coding agent Codex, Claude Code’s most direct competitor. “Together, we’ll build agents that have your back and your team’s, and keep you in control,” Wu wrote on X. Last month, Apple quietly lowered the daily AI spending cap for some engineers to $200 from $300, and some teams could see theirs fall to as little as $100. Non-engineering groups, already limited to $100 a day, could see some caps drop as low as $25. Employees who need more can ask senior leadership for an exemption. Apple staff can use tools including Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini, and some teams are being steered toward cheaper or on-device models. The cuts come as new CEO John Ternus pushes the company to run faster and leaner, and after Apple’s R&D spending jumped 32% in fiscal 2026. That’s how much enterprises spent on AI in the year to September 2026, according to Menlo Ventures’ latest State of Enterprise AI report. The figure is more than five times the $33 billion spent a year earlier, and growth sped up from the year before too. The number of companies paying for AI rose only modestly, meaning most of the growth came from existing customers spending more.

Spending also blew out budgets. The enterprises Menlo surveyed had budgeted nearly double what they spent in 2025, but on average ended up spending two and a half times that. The researchers say AI agents are driving much of the surge. On OpenRouter, a platform developers use to access hundreds of AI models in one place, agents now generate four out of five tokens, the units of text AI models process. A few companies also get the lion's share of that money. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google take more than two-thirds of enterprise AI deployment spending. Among businesses paying to plug AI models directly into their own products and tools, Anthropic now has more than half the market, up from 40%, while Google’s share fell by more than half to 9%. #5397. Sprout Ends at Block 3,543,405: What the ZIPs Say About ZEC in Orchard and Sapling

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zcash has three older shielded pools, and only one of them has a shutdown date. On November 5, NU7 will make the 22,263 ZEC left in Sprout unspendable.

The 346,000 ZEC still in Orchard and the 420,000 ZEC in Sapling face no deadline at all.

But the Zcash specifications include one conditional warning that covers all three pools, and it has been widely misquoted. Let's go through the ZIPs to set out exactly what each document says about each pool, and what it doesn't.

Together, the three older pools hold about 788,000 ZEC. Any full node reports these balances directly through the valuePools field of its getblockchaininfo RPC, so anyone running a node can check them.

The three pools are on very different paths. Sprout has a fixed end. Orchard is closed to new deposits, but no spec sets a closing date. Sapling remains a supported pool.

Sprout's end has been planned for years. ZIP 211, written in 2019, stopped new value from entering Sprout. It described that as "a step toward being able to remove the Sprout shielded protocol."

ZIP 2003 takes the final step. It doesn't target Sprout directly. Instead, it bans an entire transaction format: from NU7 onward, "the transaction version number MUST be 5 or 6." Sprout transfers can only be written as version 4 transactions, so Sprout funds can no longer be spent.

ZIP 259, the NU7 deployment spec, sets the activation height at block 3,543,405 on mainnet. It states the result directly: "funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The wording matters. ZIP 2003 says it does not "unissue, burn, or otherwise make Sprout funds permanently unavailable." The coins stay counted in Zcash's issued supply, and the ZIP leaves open "the theoretical possibility of re-enabling v4 transactions, or of adding another facility to retrieve these funds." It also cautions that this "may never be re-enabled."

Recovering Sprout funds was already hard before the deadline. According to ZIP 2003, the retirement of zcashd just before NU6.3 "removed the only maintained software that still provided wallet functionality for Sprout." The pool has barely changed in the last few weeks: the widely reported figure of 22,309 ZEC has fallen only to 22,263, so about 46 ZEC has moved out since.

Orchard's situation is newer and more unusual. ZIP 258 activated NU6.3 at block 3,428,143 and sealed Orchard after a soundness vulnerability was found and fixed. Since then, the consensus rules have enforced three restrictions:

ZIP 229 explains why: Orchard held "a substantial portion of ZEC" when the vulnerability was fixed, so moving those funds to a fresh pool was meant to restore confidence in Zcash's total supply.

The migration has largely worked. ZecStats counts 3,278,499 ZEC moved out of Orchard, about 90.5% of what was in the pool at NU6.3. That leaves about 346,000 ZEC, roughly 2% of the circulating supply.

Sapling has the fewest restrictions of the three. Version 6 transactions support it as one of the "supported shielded pools," alongside Orchard and Ironwood, and none of the NU6.3 or NU7 ZIPs restricts it.

There's one catch for Sapling users that many people are missing. ZIP 259 says the version 4 ban covers "all version 4 transactions, including transparent-only and Sapling transactions, not only Sprout transfers." Sapling funds stay spendable after NU7, but only through version 5 or version 6 transactions. Wallets still building version 4 transactions need to switch before the upgrade. Pending or offline-signed version 4 transactions won't confirm afterward, and "re-signing alone cannot make a version 4 transaction valid."

The sentence behind the "inaccessible funds" headlines appears in ZIP 2005, "Ironwood Quantum Recoverability," and is repeated in ZIP 229:

"Recovery would not be possible for funds still in the Sprout, Sapling, or Orchard pools; all such funds would be inaccessible after their respective protocols are disabled."

The sentence before it explains the context. Zcash's existing shielded protocols depend on discrete logarithms being hard to compute. If an attacker, using a quantum computer or another method, could break that, the protocols might have to be disabled "to prevent such attacks." Only funds in Ironwood would be recoverable, through a recovery protocol designed to stay secure against quantum attacks.

So this is a contingency, not a schedule. It describes what would happen to funds in the older pools if a future cryptographic emergency forced Zcash to shut them down. No ZIP proposes doing that on any date. The practical advice behind it is plain: funds in Sprout, Sapling or Orchard "should be migrated to the Ironwood pool" to be covered by recovery.

The software is ready. The Zcash Foundation released Zebra 7.0.0 on October 22. Its changelog says it "supports the NU7 network upgrade on Mainnet, which activates at height 3,543,405." The release moves Zebra's database from format v28 to v29. Zebra 6.x can't read the new format, so the Foundation recommends backing up the old state first. The zcashd compatibility sidecar must also be updated to zebra-compat-v1.3.0. Earlier builds can't follow mainnet past NU7.

This upgrade carries more risk than usual. ZIP 259 waives Zcash's usual rule that old software must shut itself down before an upgrade. The spec warns that "operators of unsupported software may therefore remain online at activation and follow a pre-NU7 consensus branch."

For holders, the guidance from each pool's spec comes down to this:

On November 5, Sprout closes. The 766,000 ZEC in Sapling and Orchard face no deadline, but the specs still recommend moving it to Ironwood.

#5396. Google’s Message to Schools K-12: If You Ban AI, You’ll Lose Access to Google Search

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI tools will be off by default for students in 2027, but districts that opt out entirely won’t have access to search tools.

Google is fine with giving schools more control over its AI tools for students, but there’s one big catch: Schools that block AI entirely will also lose student access to Google Search, The New York Times reports.

Starting early next year, Google will turn off its AI tools for K-12 students by default unless administrators opt in. But since search now comes with AI built in, schools that keep AI off will lose search, too. This new policy comes as pushback grows. In September, New York City and LA, both Google clients, limited student access to generative AI, and New York State just passed a chatbot safety law for minors.

“Search and A.I. are deeply integrated,” Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president for education, explains. For districts that allow AI, students will get one of two search options: standard Google Search with AI Overviews, or a tutoring-style version powered by Guided Learning, a Gemini feature built to walk students through topics step by step instead of handing them answers.

Not everyone gives the new plan an A. Former FTC Chair Lina Khan says Google is using its “search monopoly to coerce schools” into adopting its AI, according to the Times.

#5395. How the Democratic party flipped the House and Senate, in 12 charts

The 2026 midterm race results saw a blue wave that secured a Democrat majority in both the Senate and House of Representatives. They flipped Senate seats in states the party hadn’t won in decades and took back a House that Republicans had controlled since 2023.

But what led to the turnaround that had voters turn out?

The Democratic party needed a net gain of four seats to win back the Senate, and many in the party had seen 2026 as a testing ground.

“What we’re seeing in the early parts of 2026 really puts Democrats in a good position, as long as we don’t screw it up,” Jen O’Malley Dillon, a Democratic campaign strategist, said at a Dartmouth political event in April. “It’s never been more complex to find a way to reach people. We are such a polarized country when it comes to our politics and, and, you know, people are tuning out in a lot of ways and for good reason—because we need to survive.”

In a stunning showing, Democrats flipped seven Senate seats in North Carolina, South Carolina, Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio and Maine.

Several of the wins came in what were once considered Republican strongholds. Kansas hadn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in almost 100 years, and a surge in turnout helped Democrats win across the South.

The Senate control means Democrats have an effective veto over President Donald Trump’s nominees for the rest of his term.

All 435 House seats were on the ballot, and Democrats went in holding 214. The party then went on to flip 25 Republican seats, and CBS estimates the party could reach 259 seats—well above the 218 Republicans held going in.

Wins came in battleground districts in North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Texas, Michigan, New York, Ohio, Kentucky, and Colorado.

Trump wasn’t on the ballot, but many voters treated the election as a referendum on him. Across age demographics, voters said their vote in Congress was to show opposition to Trump about 39% to 60%, while only 7% to 22% said they voted to show support.

The opposition vote was strongest among the youngest voters—60% of 18- to 29-year olds voted with intent to oppose Trump. Voters 65 and older were the most likely to say they were backing Trump (22%), but even that group leaned toward opposition. Trump himself claimed Republicans would have “won IN A LANDSLIDE” if he had been on the ballot, according to his Truth Social post.

Trump went into election day near the bottom of historical presidential approval. His most recent reading on the presidential approval rating sat at 29%, from Oct. 20. That’s the lowest for any president since George W. Bush fell to 25% in October 2008 during the financial crisis.

Democrats won every age group under 65. Voters 18 to 29 backed Democratic House candidates 72% to Republican candidates’ 25%—but they made up only 11% of the electorate. That’s a sharp turn from 2024, when the youngest voters were roughly split between Trump and Kamala Harris.

The bigger gains came from the middle of the voting population. Voters aged 30 to 44 went Democratic 60% to 36%, and voters 45 to 64—the second largest group at 34%—went 51% to 47%. Only voters 65 and older, the largest group at 35%, narrowly favored Republicans 51% to 48%.

Concern about the economy remained a flashpoint among voters. About four in 10 named the economy as the most important issue facing the country—with the highest shares coming from Black voters (50%) and voters aged 30 to 44 (45%).

The issue a voter named as most important was a strong predictor of their vote. About eight in 10 voters who said the state of democracy was the top issue backed the Democratic House candidate, while immigration was the clearest Republican issue—89% of those voters backed the GOP. Both Democrat and Republicans were close to evenly split on the economy.

Many voters perceived that Congress is not doing enough to check Trump’s presidential powers. Among voters who disapprove of Trump, 94% felt that way. Voters who approved of him were divided.

But neither branch has much public trust. In July, only 4% of adults had a great deal of confidence in the people running Congress, and 53% had hardly any.

The executive branch fared slightly better in public perception, but it still had weak support. With both chambers flipping, Democrats now control what Congress investigates—as the majority now gives the party oversight on presidential powers.

The new Senate class includes several historic firsts: Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed will be the first Muslim U.S. senator, Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan will be the first Native American woman in the Senate, New Hampshire’s Chris Pappas will be the first openly gay man elected to the chamber, Iowa’s Josh Turek will be the first Paralympian senator and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews will be the first woman elected to the Senate from her state.

In Kansas, Adam Hamilton became the state’s first Democratic senator since 1932. And in Texas, James Talarico beat Ken Paxton—ending a 38-year Democrat drought in the state’s Senate seat and overcoming Elon Musk’s $212 million effort.

Wall Street rallied overall following the midterm results. The S&P 500 was up 1.8% Wednesday morning and the DOW gained more than 1,000 points—but companies tied to Trump, Musk, and the AI buildout moved the other way.

Meanwhile, Trump Media fell 11.7%, adding to a 55% loss for the year. Musk had donated heavily to Republicans during the campaign, and both Tesla and SpaceX fell. Data center power providers took some hits as well: Vistra was down 9.6% and Vertiv 8.7%. Defense contractors including Lockheed Martin and L3Harris lost about 4%.

Joshua Hong is a News Fellow at Fortune covering data, AI, cybersecurity, energy, and retail.

#5394. Amazon plans its first large-scale data centers in Washington state as residents raise concerns

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:46 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:36 am

Amazon is moving toward building its first large-scale data centers in Washington state, with a proposed campus in Walla Walla County and a second in the Tri-Cities that the company confirmed this week.

The expansion into Amazon’s home state comes amid nationwide pushback against the rapid deployment of new AI data centers. Tuesday’s election underscored the scrutiny facing data center developers, with voters in communities across several states backing limits on new projects. In Eastern Washington, the Amazon proposals have drawn calls for greater environmental oversight and a temporary halt to data center development.

Amazon already has a substantial footprint in neighboring Oregon, where industry tracker Baxtel lists 64 AWS data center sites. Expansion there has divided communities, with residents pushing for restrictions over power and water concerns while some Eastern Oregon officials warn that slowing development would jeopardize jobs and tax revenue.

Both proposed Washington campuses would initially include three data center buildings. The Walla Walla County site covers roughly 134 acres in Wallula Gap, while the Tri-Cities campus is on a 1,000 acre property in the city of West Richland and could eventually grow to 21 buildings. The company is already operating smaller data centers in the state, including Seattle.

The Tri-City Herald first reported Monday that Amazon was behind the West Richland project. The company plans to hold a community open house Nov. 19 to discuss the proposal.

A full build-out of the West Richland campus could create more than 1,000 full-time data center jobs, Amazon said. Dallas real estate firm Trammell Crow initially purchased the property from the estate of agricultural businessman Frank Tiegs, who died in 2024, before selling it to Amazon.

Nearby residents have raised concerns about the planned campus, in part because of its proximity to about 200 homes. Residents asked the local city council to approve a temporary moratorium, but at a meeting Tuesday evening, council members adopted rules that removed a data center noise exemption, banned them in light industrial zones, and prohibited cryptocurrency mining. The council failed to pass a moratorium, NonStop Local reported.

Amazon says the upcoming open house will give residents an opportunity to ask questions about the planned development. A spokesperson described a “science fair” format, with booths hosted by experts discussing water and energy usage, job creation, noise and environmental impacts.

“We’re committed to growing responsibly and we want the community to leave the Open House with a better understanding of this project and what it could mean for the area,” the spokesperson said via email.

At Wallula Gap, a recent public-comment period offers an indication of the scrutiny Amazon faces.

Of the 706 submissions received during a 30-day comment period that closed Oct. 12, only 23 — about 3% — supported the project, according to an analysis by the Walla Walla Union-Bulletin. Most of the supportive comments came from the area, and many predicated their support on more stringent oversight of the proposed facility near the Columbia River.

More than 500 submissions came from outside Walla Walla County, according to the Union-Bulletin. Many included template language calling for an Environmental Impact Statement — a higher level of environmental assessment than currently required for the campus.

The proposed facility is located at the Wallula Gap Business Park, on property formerly owned by the Port of Walla Walla. The three proposed single-story data center buildings would create approximately 120 to 150 full-time jobs, Amazon said.

The land is zoned for “industrial agriculture – mixed” applications, which the company said includes data centers. Amazon’s involvement in the project was first reported by the Tri-City Herald in February.

Amazon’s FAQs for the two sites address several issues raised by residents, including electricity costs and water use.

Rising electric bills nationwide and the climate impacts of new gas power plants and backup diesel generators have made energy use a top concern. Amazon said it will work with local utilities and other officials “to ensure that our data centers do not raise electricity bills for people in our communities.”

The company reports that it matched all electricity consumed across its global operations with renewable energy sources in 2023 and 2024. That annual, company-wide accounting measure does not mean each facility runs on renewable electricity around the clock.

Amazon also points to its investment of “billions of dollars in nuclear energy projects,” including a proposed small modular reactor plant near the Tri-Cities that could come online in the 2030s.

“This project will provide net-new carbon-free energy for communities in the Pacific Northwest, including Eastern Washington,” Amazon said in its FAQ.

Amid concerns about water shortages, Amazon touts water-use rates that it says beat other tech companies and are much lower than irrigated farming. Those rates, however, do not include water used in electricity generation. Many power plants use water to produce steam that drives electricity-generating turbines and for cooling, with some water lost through evaporation.

At both locations, Amazon says it will pay 100% of its property taxes rather than seek tax breaks for building in the communities. The company says its taxes are higher than most industrial uses and directly support schools, roads, fire and police, and other services.

Beyond addressing concerns about its data centers, Amazon is making a broader case for why communities should welcome them. Last month, the company launched its Built Together initiative, committing more than $1 billion in additional investments over five years to U.S. communities where it operates data centers. The funding supports efforts including free community college, energy upgrades for homes and buildings, and workforce training.

In announcing the program, Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman framed data center development as part of a global race for AI dominance. He warned that local and state moratoriums could harm the U.S. economy and national security.

“If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” Garman said. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.”

In West Richland, residents will have an opportunity to question Amazon’s plans — and the assurances accompanying them — at the company’s upcoming open house.

Editor’s note: Story updated 11/5 to note that Amazon is operating smaller-scale data centers in Washington, but not campuses of the scope being proposed in Eastern Washington.

#5393. These 5 AI Prompts Can Take Over the Marketing Tasks That Eat Up Your Week

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Copy these ready-made prompts into your favorite AI tool and get hours of your week back for the work that actually grows your business.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Running a business means wearing a lot of hats, and marketing is a common one that slips. You know you need a content calendar, a steady blog, ad creative, and emails people actually open. Finding the hours to build all of it from scratch is the hard part.

AI prompts help with that. A good prompt hands you a first draft of the thinking work: a month of post topics, a blog outline, a stack of headlines to test. While you make the calls, the AI gets you past that blank page so you can get moving.

The prompts below cover tasks that eat up a small team’s week: planning content, outlining blog posts, writing ad copy, testing email subject lines, and researching competitors. Each one comes with the prompt itself, what it does, who it’s for, which AI tools it works with, and steps for using it.

Copy the prompt, swap your details into the brackets, and run it. The follow-up steps are where the real shaping happens, so don’t skip them. Check every result against what you know about your business and your customers before you publish anything. AI works from patterns, so it can miss details only you have.

The Prompt: “Act as a content strategist for a [industry] business. Build a 30-day social media content calendar for [platform]. Mix educational posts, behind-the-scenes posts, and promotional posts at roughly a 3:1:1 ratio. For each day, give me a topic and a one-line angle, not a full caption. Flag any days where a seasonal event, holiday, or industry moment could shape the topic.”

What It Does: This prompt turns a blank content plan into 30 ready-to-write topics in one pass. It keeps the mix balanced, so promotional posts don’t crowd out the content readers actually want, and it surfaces timely hooks you might otherwise miss while planning weeks in advance.

Who It’s For: Founders juggling their own social media without a marketing team behind them, plus small teams who split content duties across two or three people and need one shared plan to work from.

The Prompt: “Act as an SEO content strategist. I’m writing a blog post targeting the keyword ‘[target keyword]’ for an audience of [audience]. Give me a title, a meta description under 155 characters, and an outline with H2 and H3 headers that covers what a searcher expects to find. Flag any subtopics competitors likely already cover.”

What It Does: This prompt saves the research phase of blog writing by mapping out structure and gaps before a single sentence gets drafted.

Who It’s For: Marketing teams and solo bloggers who write regularly but don’t have time for a full competitive audit on every post.

The Prompt: “Act as a direct-response copywriter. Write 8 short ad headlines and 4 primary text variations for [product/service], targeting [audience]. Each headline should lead with a different angle: a pain point, a benefit, a number, and a question. Keep headlines under 40 characters.”

What It Does: This prompt gives you a stack of testable ad variations in minutes instead of staring at a blank headline field.

Who It’s For: Anyone running their own paid social or search campaigns without an in-house copywriter.

The Prompt: “Act as an email marketer. Here’s my current subject line: ‘[insert subject line]’. Give me 6 alternatives that increase curiosity or urgency without sounding like clickbait. For each one, explain in one sentence why it might outperform the original.”

What It Does: This prompt takes a flat subject line and turns it into a set of sharper, testable options, along with the reasoning behind each one.

Who It’s For: Newsletter writers and small marketing teams who send regularly but rarely A/B test subject lines.

The Prompt: “Act as a market research analyst. I compete with [competitor name(s)] in the [industry] space. Based on what you know about their positioning, list 5 topics or content angles they likely haven’t covered well, and explain the opportunity for each.”

What It Does: This prompt surfaces content and positioning gaps a competitor has left open, giving you a shortlist of angles worth owning first.

Who It’s For: Founders and marketers trying to differentiate in a crowded niche.

Running a business means wearing a lot of hats, and marketing is a common one that slips. You know you need a content calendar, a steady blog, ad creative, and emails people actually open. Finding the hours to build all of it from scratch is the hard part.

AI prompts help with that. A good prompt hands you a first draft of the thinking work: a month of post topics, a blog outline, a stack of headlines to test. While you make the calls, the AI gets you past that blank page so you can get moving.

The prompts below cover tasks that eat up a small team’s week: planning content, outlining blog posts, writing ad copy, testing email subject lines, and researching competitors. Each one comes with the prompt itself, what it does, who it’s for, which AI tools it works with, and steps for using it.

#5392. U.S. Hotels Just Booked 7.5 Million Extra Room Nights in 6 Weeks. That Hasn’t Happened Since 2011.

Record fall bookings could make 2026 the biggest year ever for U.S. hotels. Luxury properties and convention cities are leading the charge.

America’s hotels can’t keep their rooms empty. Since Labor Day, they’ve sold 7.5 million more room nights than in the same weeks last year. That’s the largest six-week jump in hotel demand since 2011 outside the pandemic recovery, according to STR data published by CoStar.

So who’s booking? Mainly conventions and business groups. Chicago led major markets with a 39.7% jump in revenue per available room during the week of Oct. 18-24, fueled by PACK EXPO at McCormick Place. Las Vegas rose 25.8% on the back of the FABTECH trade show, and New York City hit 93.6% occupancy, its highest since 2024, thanks to overlapping conferences, events and leisure travel.

Luxury and upper-upscale hotels posted a combined 13.4% gain. Economy properties, a segment that includes Super 8 and Days Inn, were the only class to miss double digits, at 8.8%.

If the trend holds, STR says 2026 will likely be the biggest year for U.S. hotel demand on record. That’s good news for brands like Hampton by Hilton, the No. 1 lodging franchise on Entrepreneur’s Franchise 500 for 17 straight years.

#5391. Ai2 gets $5M from Google to turn AI weather model into a tool for projecting climate change

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 5, 2026 at 2:27 pm

Google is giving Seattle’s Allen Institute for AI about $5 million in funding, plus another $1.8 million in cloud credits, to turn an AI weather model developed by Google Research into a tool for projecting climate change decades into the future.

The money will help Ai2 build an open-source model designed to give scientists, water agencies and other planners a faster, more accurate look at how rainfall, temperatures and water supplies could change over the next five to 50 years.

Announced Wednesday morning, the three-year project pairs funding from Google.org, the company’s philanthropic arm, with technical support from Google Research. Ai2 will add four people to its eight-person climate modeling team to do the work.

Google’s work on the model centers on weather, looking ahead a year at most. It has less interest and expertise in climate projections that run decades into the future, said Oliver Watt-Meyer, Ai2’s director of research for AI climate modeling.

“Climate modeling is a bit more of a public good,” he said. “It is information that people need to know, but it’s often more government agencies that are thinking about this.”

Starting with Google’s model: Ai2’s model, NeuralGCM+, will build on Google’s NeuralGCM, which mixes traditional physics equations with AI. Watt-Meyer, who wrote about NeuralGCM for the journal Nature when Google published its research in 2024, said the model does well at forecasting weather and at recreating past climate.

In that piece, he also pointed out its limits: some of its long runs broke down, and when researchers simulated ocean temperatures about 7 degrees Fahrenheit warmer than today, its predictions for the atmosphere didn’t make physical sense.

Under the new project, Ai2 will try to fix both problems. It will connect NeuralGCM+ to an ocean and sea ice model, with the goal of running stable simulations that span decades. It will also build more established physics into the model, then check its predictions for a warmer world against results from traditional climate models.

Ai2’s climate team is made up largely of atmospheric scientists, with the engineers and computing power of an AI institute behind them.

Ai2 is “uniquely positioned to extend Google’s NeuralGCM model into the next generation of long-term climate projections,” said Alex Diaz, head of applied science at Google.org, in a statement, citing the institute’s climate science expertise and commitment to open research.

Where the idea started: The team’s origins go back to the late Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen, who took an interest in climate modeling before his death in 2018. His company, then known as Vulcan, launched the climate modeling project in 2019, and the group moved to Ai2 in 2021. Allen had founded the nonprofit AI institute in 2014.

The original plan was to combine physics and AI. The group set that aside because the AI couldn’t be trained well inside older climate models written in Fortran, a decades-old programming language. Google wrote NeuralGCM in modern code that solves that problem.

In that way, Watt-Meyer said, “This is actually kind of coming full circle for us.”

Ai2 already has its own family of AI climate models, called the Ai2 Climate Emulator, or ACE. These models rely entirely on AI and run much faster than NeuralGCM. But versions trained only on historical data struggle to project a climate the planet hasn’t experienced yet.

Watt-Meyer said NeuralGCM’s design could hold up better as the world warms, because the laws of physics built into it won’t change.

The timeline: The first step is releasing the code for training NeuralGCM, which has been tied to Google’s internal systems. Making it public will let other researchers train their own versions, including on common GPUs rather than only Google’s own chips. Ai2 expects to release it within the first year, with work on the ocean model running in parallel.

Making the model reliable in a warmer world is the hardest part, and it could take longer than three years. “We don’t know if it’ll work necessarily,” Watt-Meyer said.

He said AI coding agents are changing what his team thinks it can get done in that time. The tools are well suited to translating old code into modern programming languages. In one case, an outside group converted a well-known ocean model from Fortran into the same language NeuralGCM uses, so Ai2 won’t have to build its own.

Watt-Meyer called the tools “a real game changer” for simulation. “It’s kind of a golden era for this kind of scientific computing,” he said.

Google Research will keep developing NeuralGCM for forecasts of a few weeks to a year, and the two teams will share training code and data. One of Google’s lead NeuralGCM researchers is spending three days at Ai2 this week.

Who would use the model: Watt-Meyer pointed to questions such as how rainfall could change in the Southwest, a key issue for water planning around Lake Powell on the Colorado River. Insurance and reinsurance companies already use Ai2’s ACE models in their research.

Asked whether data center developers could use these kinds of models, Watt-Meyer said they could help answer questions about cooling, access to renewable energy and risks such as extreme weather and rising seas. But it isn’t clear if the industry is paying attention.

“There’s so much frantic energy to build these things as fast as possible,” he said. “I’m not sure people are really seriously considering this kind of climate data, though maybe they should be a bit more.”

Correction: An earlier version of this story gave an incorrect date for the start of the climate modeling effort at Vulcan. It started in 2019.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5390. Wall Street’s best post-midterm rally in 44 years lasted just one day—then $3 trillion vanished as chip stocks plunged over AI fears

The Nasdaq fell about 5% on Thursday and the S&P 500 nearly 4%, just a day after Wall Street had cheered the Democratic sweep of Congress.

By early Thursday afternoon, the Nasdaq dropped 5.2% and the S&P 500 3.8%, and the Dow was down 2.9%, or more than 1,500 points. The S&P 500 fell as low as 7,394.49, below where it closed on Election Day. Thursday’s drop off seemed to hit AI and tech stocks the hardest: the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index was down about 9.75% in a Reuters intraday snapshot and briefly fell as much as 11%, on track for its steepest daily loss since March 2020. Among other AI-related stocks include AMD and Micron, which each lost roughly 15%, and Nvidia fell almost 9%.

But the drop came a day late. On Wednesday, the Dow rose 1,569 points, or 3%, its best performance after a midterm election in 44 years. The S&P 500 rose 1.6% to 7,688.62, as oil fell more than 8% and investors seemed to hope that a divided government would mean steadier policy.

But by Thursday, U.S. stocks had shed roughly $3 trillion in market value, and the Dow was heading for its worst second trading day after a midterm in data going back to the index’s start in 1896.

Perhaps part of the reason for the huge hit to the AI and tech sectors could be because of the Blue Tsunami. There were 41 ballot measures regarding slowing down data center buildouts, and most of them passed, especially in Ohio. So the midterm risk to AI was showing up on Wednesday, but only in parts of the market, before it showed up in full Thursday.

Vistra plunged 14% and Vertiv fell 13% on fears of data center moratoriums, while Nvidia slipped only 3% on Wednesday. Smaller AI cloud providers such as CoreWeave were also hit hard, since a permitting slowdown in Texas would hurt operators like CoreWeave before it reached the hyperscalers that are their main customers. Meanwhile, some of the biggest tech companies—which pay for the build-out—saw their stocks rise. Some analysts and economists argued political pushback could let air out of an inevitable AI bubble without popping it.

That’s when Asian markets started selling off overnight: South Korea’s Kospi closed down 5.28% with trading halts during the session, Taiwan’s main index fell 3.2% and the Nikkei 1.79%. By Thursday, the largest U.S. tech names had joined the decline: Tesla dropped as much as 10%, Qualcomm fell 11.2% and Arm Holdings 11% after weaker technology earnings. Oil prices also rebounded following Wednesday’s drop.

While the losses were most concentrated in tech, four of the S&P 500’s 11 sectors were up on the day, including consumer staples, which rose 1.5%, and Berkshire Hathaway hit an all-time high.

Texas is the main source of worry about the build-out. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who wants an immediate moratorium on new data centers, beat Republican Gov. Greg Abbott—Wells Fargo estimates 27% of planned data center gigawatts are in Texas. Amy Acton in Ohio and Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia also campaigned on restricting data center development.

The opposition is not purely partisan. Abbott paused new data center permits in September pending a grid audit, and Hinojosa campaigned on extending that moratorium. Hinojosa likely won’t need a new law, since Abbott’s pause on grid connections already freezes data center permits.

Catherina covers markets, the economy, energy, tech, and AI.

#5389. Do Gift Guides Actually Work for PR? Here’s the Honest Answer

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Gift guides can be one of the best PR tools for product brands. They put you in front of shoppers who are looking for ideas and ready to buy, and they build trust fast.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Every year around this time, I get the same call from founders seeking whether a gift guide placement is possible. Usually, the answer is no. And that’s the first lesson. Gift guide season starts months before the holidays, when most brands are still thinking about summer. Editors are building their lists while you’re at the beach.But the real question behind that call is bigger: are gift guides even worth the effort? Or are they just a fancy way of buying ad space? I’ve seen both sides, so my take is simple. Gift guides are one of the most useful PR tools a product brand has, but only when you use them for the right reason. Let’s get into it.

Start with the obvious. People are in buying mode. Someone reading a gift guide isn’t casually scrolling. They have a person to shop for and a budget in mind. Some are really looking for what to gift. They’re looking for ideas or to be pointed toward something they didn’t know existed.Then there’s trust. When a respected outlet puts your product on a list, it’s a recommendation, not a sales pitch. Readers know the difference, even if they can’t explain it.Here’s what that can look like in practice:• Direct sales. A strong placement can send traffic and orders within hours of publishing• Third-party credibility. “As seen in” works because someone else said it first• Long-term search value. Many guides stay live for years and keep sending visitors• Relationship building. The editor who includes you in November may call you for a trend story in March.That’s a big deal for lesser-known brands. Nobody searches for a name they’ve never heard of. Last year, I worked with an up-and-coming oral-care brand and placed its products in gift guides across the board, including those from bloggers, tier-1 publications and trade magazines. The founder told me their online sales were up 30% compared to the same period the year before.A guide puts you in front of people who weren’t looking for you but were ready to buy.

Now the uncomfortable part. Not every gift guide is earned. Some are paid placements dressed up as editorial. Some are affiliate-driven, meaning the outlet earns money when you make a sale. Others charge a participation fee just to be considered.Is that wrong? Not always. But it’s advertising, and you should call it that. If you pay for it, measure it like an ad. Look at cost per sale, not just a pretty logo on your website.The reality is even earned placements don’t always sell. A guide at a tier-1 publication with 50 products on it is a crowded room. Your item might get a thumbnail and a one-line description.I’ve watched brands celebrate a big-name feature and then see almost nothing in their sales dashboard. It hurts.I once had a client who wrote a marketing book. I landed it in a well-known gift guide, and she was thrilled. She shared the placement everywhere and used it to keep promoting the book. But the sales told a different story. She barely saw the needle move from that one placement.

I see the same mistakes over and over.• They pitch too late. Print and long-lead outlets plan five to six months ahead. Even digital editors start early. If you pitch in November, you’re already behind.• They send generic pitches. “Our product is perfect for the holidays!” tells an editor nothing. What’s the gift? Who is it for? What’s the price? Why now?• They ignore the category. A guide for “Gifts for Dads” has different needs than “Gifts Under $50.” Pitch the right one.• They forget the landing page. This one is expensive. A reader clicks through and lands on your homepage with no gift context, no bundle and no clear next step. They leave.

If you want results, treat it like a campaign, not a lucky break.Here’s an example from my own work. Last summer, I helped a client land a spot at a media event for gift-guide editors. He showed up with his product and handed out plenty of samples to the journalists in attendance.We also made the pitch easy to act on. The pamphlet held only the key points, starting with the price, so editors building “Gifts Under $20” or “Gifts Under $50” lists could spot a fit right away. We made the word “Household” stand out so they’d know which category it belonged in. And we spelled out why the product mattered and what difference it would make in someone’s daily life.Then we added a QR code. It linked to everything an editor might need: product details, descriptions and photos. If they decided to include the product, all they had to do was copy and paste.The result? Placements in both broadcast and print outlets.

Gift guides aren’t magic. They won’t save a weak product, but for the right brand, with the right timing, they’re one of the few PR tactics that can build trust and drive revenue in the same breath. That’s a rare combination.So don’t ask, “Do gift guides work?” Ask, “Am I ready for one to work?”If the answer is yes, start planning now. Next year’s lists are already being built in the heads of the editors you want to reach.

#5388. Asia can’t afford a ‘cloudless’ day. That means paying attention to undersea cables

Kapil Kumar Jain is vice president of global network services at Tata Communications.

Picture a “cloudless” day—not in the meteorological sense, but one in which digital operations come to a sudden, catastrophic halt. Financial transactions stall. AI applications lose access to data. Supply chains slow, and customer experiences suffer.

It may sound improbable, yet recent events suggest otherwise. In 2024, subsea cable damage caused widespread internet outages that disrupted banks, fintech platforms and cloud-based businesses across Africa; in 2025, Red Sea cable cuts severely disrupted access across Asia and the Middle East. Internet traffic was rerouted through longer paths, increasing latency for cloud services and adding costs for businesses reliant on real-time digital operations.

These incidents are a reminder that what we call “the cloud” is neither virtual nor invincible. We often imagine it floating somewhere above us. In reality, it lies at the bottom of the ocean: More than 99% of all international data is carried not by satellites but by a physical backbone of subsea cables.

The regional digital economy runs uninterrupted only because companies made continuous, heavy investment in critical transit hubs like India and Singapore.

AI is placing unprecedented demands on the cloud, the foundation of today’s digital economy. AI workloads and hyperscale data centres need ever-greater bandwidth—with 400 gigabits (gbps) per second now the baseline and 800 gbps already emerging.

As countries and businesses race to scale AI, much of the focus has been on compute and data centres. But the networks connecting those systems need to keep pace as well. That raises a critical question for Asia: is the region overlooking a key AI infrastructure bottleneck?

Without sufficient investment in subsea cables and end-to-end networks, businesses could spend heavily on AI infrastructure only to see the returns eroded by disruption, higher operating costs and unreliable access to data.

For the C-suite, that presents a looming crisis: while AI investment is a board-level strategic priority for 77% of enterprise leaders, 65% of enterprises continue to operate on legacy or still-developing infrastructure, according to a Tata Communications study.

With AI workloads making global traffic patterns increasingly unpredictable, enterprises need dynamic, flexible data-centre-to-data-centre connectivity that can scale rapidly with demand to protect the bottom line and operational stability. Meeting this need will require continued investment from network providers in the infrastructure and capabilities needed to deliver scalable, resilient connectivity.

Most discussions of Singapore’s AI ambitions revolve around compute capacity, talent and regulation. Those are all important. But they overlook what happens when the data that AI systems depend on cannot be transmitted quickly, reliably or securely.

Singapore and India are emerging as two of the region’s most important data transit hubs, underpinned by their strategic locations and growing digital infrastructure. Singapore serves as a gateway to Southeast Asia, with one of the world’s densest concentrations of data centres. Meanwhile, India acts as a link between Asia, the Middle East and Europe, supported by major cable landing points and expanding data centre capacity in cities such as Mumbai and Chennai. Together, these strengths make both countries important hubs for international data traffic, underscoring the need for resilient and diverse connectivity routes to keep data moving efficiently between major financial centres and commercial workloads.

The industry needs to rethink how it approaches network architecture. For decades, infrastructure was built to support predictable, linear traffic. Today, infrastructure must now accommodate increasingly volatile AI-driven data demands.

This requires better integration  between subsea cables, terrestrial fibre and individual data centres, as a bottleneck at a coastal landing station can immediately negate the speed of a transoceanic cable.

However, keeping these cables secure and running requires far more than laying fiber in the ocean. True resilience demands a coordinated focus across four dimensions: capacity planning, network diversity, protection and repair readiness, and disciplined lifecycle operations.

This behind-the-scenes management—including robust monitoring, strategic spares management, tight integration of subsea and terrestrial networks, and clearly defined long-term governance—is what ensures a single cable cut does not become a regional blackout.

Crucially, this industry-led push is now being reinforced by public policy. The recent adoption of the Enhanced ASEAN Guidelines for Strengthening Resilience and Repair of Submarine Cables—which recommends capping repair processing times at 10 days—is a vital step forward. Regional policymakers are making rapid repair readiness of economic stability.

For businesses,  the practical consequence is a change in what gets funded. Compute and data centres often take priority in investment decisions because their capacity and returns are visible. Meanwhile, the cables, landing stations and alternative routes that keep them connected are less visible, and can be harder to justify as investments in their own right. Yet, the trade-off is clear: underinvestment in connectivity risks leaving expensive AI infrastructure vulnerable to disruption, congestion and higher operating costs. Connectivity must be treated as an essential and strategic asset not simply an operational cost hidden in the IT budget. The cloud begins beneath the ocean. As AI adoption accelerates, Singapore’s competitiveness as a global digital hub will depend on the strength of that invisible lifeline beneath the sea.

#5387. First X-BAT fighter jet prototype unveiled as Shield AI preps Seattle area factory for 2027 launch

by John Cook on Nov 4, 2026 at 8:26 amNovember 4, 2026 at 8:41 am

Defense technology startup Shield AI has completed its first full-scale prototype of the X-BAT autonomous fighter jet as the company prepares its manufacturing and engineering hub south of Seattle.

Constructed in 12 months at a facility in Frisco, Texas, the prototype is currently en route to the company’s flight-test center at Newton City-County Airport in Kansas.

The milestone keeps Shield AI on track for its major manufacturing push in the Seattle area, one that it says could employ 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s.

In late September, the company announced a 420,000-square-foot facility dubbed “X-Forge 3” at the Des Moines Creek Business Park, which is scheduled to open in spring 2027. The company has already posted dozens of Seattle-area job openings across avionics, mechanical design, software engineering and aircraft manufacturing.

The unveiling of the X-BAT prototype keeps the company on schedule for its planned regional buildout in Des Moines, a spokesperson tells GeekWire.

“This milestone represents a year of sustained effort and discipline from a team that committed to an ambitious design and build schedule and delivered,” Armor Harris, senior vice president of aircraft engineering at Shield AI, said in a blog post. “That is no small feat.”

San Diego-based Shield AI expects the first X-BAT aircraft to roll off the line in Des Moines in 2028, with full production ramping up to about 150 aircraft per year by the early 2030s, Harris told GeekWire in an interview in September.

It’s an extremely ambitious timeline, but one the company says is necessary given the changing dynamics of warfare.

“The team is laser focused on keeping pace because we know a capability is only useful if it arrives in time to matter,” Harris said. “We cannot take decades to develop an aircraft when the need is already here. That urgency has shaped how we approach the engineering work, and how we work with partners in the U.S. government.”

Unveiled last year, the X-BAT is an AI-piloted strike fighter that takes off and lands vertically, carries up to 2,000-pound class weapons in internal bays, and is designed for a 1,000-nautical-mile combat radius — which, when it takes flight, would top the estimated 590 nautical mile combat radius of the Lockheed Martin F-35A.

One of its key tactical advantages is the ability to take off and land without concrete runways — hence the tagline for the X-BAT: “Earth is our Runway.”

The X-BAT launches from and returns to a mobile, trailer-mounted Launch and Recovery Vehicle, which allows the AI-piloted jet to deploy from cargo ships, naval destroyers or remote areas where it’s too costly or dangerous to build traditional runways.

“Our adversaries have invested in long range missiles that put our aircraft at risk when they’re on the ground. Aircraft are hard to shoot down in the air, but easy to destroy when they’re on the ground,” Harris notes in the blog post. “X-BAT is the answer to this threat because it forces the adversary to take all those assets that are overhead looking down at our airbases and makes them try to go and find where the X-BATs are hiding.”

Last month, the U.S. Navy awarded Shield AI a $150 million contract modification through the Pentagon’s Defense Exportability Features program, matched dollar-for-dollar by $150 million in private Shield AI funds. Alongside a prior $100 million joint Navy and Defense Innovation Unit award in August, total program backing stands at approximately $400 million.

Co-founded by former Navy SEAL Brandon Tseng, Shield AI raised a $2 billion venture capital round at a $12.7 billion valuation earlier this year.

With the prototype built, Shield AI’s engineering team is focusing on proving out its vertical-takeoff-and-landing mechanics in Kansas ahead of initial flight trials later this year.

Harris detailed a multi-phase testing campaign ahead:

“We’ve built the first aircraft,” Harris wrote. “Now it’s time to go prove what it can do.”

#5386. I Dropped Out of Harvard to Start a Company That Lets You Copy Successful Investors. It’s Powered $2B in Trades.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Steven Wang wants everyday investors to learn from the best and grow their wealth.

This as-told-to story is based on a conversation with Steven Wang, founder and CEO of Dub, a social investing platform that allows everyday investors to follow verified Wall Street professionals and wealth managers and automatically mirror their strategies. Wang left high school to build, fund and sell a VR startup called Realism. By age 18, Apple had hired him as an engineering product manager. He went on to attend Harvard before dropping out to focus on Dub, which has powered $2 billion in trades. The piece has been edited for length and clarity.

My parents immigrated here from China. We didn’t have a lot of money growing up, so money was always a big topic in the family. I started hustling on the playground: just doing business here and there, selling Pokémon cards, etc. That got me interested in financial markets. I read a couple of the early books from Ben Graham and Warren Buffett. Then I asked my parents to open me a custodial trading account in second grade. They loaned me $200.

I remember losing a lot of money in those early days. It was still $7 a trade before Robinhood. But it was so cool, this concept of ownership in a company, no matter how small it was. In many ways, it was the first time I really realized the American dream. That was super inspiring for me as a kid, and I continued to invest.

Early on, I got into technology too, through robotics. I ended up starting my first company, in virtual reality, during my sophomore year of high school. It was my first time leaving home, raising venture capital. We actually sold the business, and that was the first time I made some real money as a kid. So that led me to go work for Apple. I was the youngest person on our team. Then I decided to go to college.

I started at Harvard in the fall of 2020. Not a great time to start school. The pandemic had just hit. Classes were on Zoom. And the markets were starting to get really frothy. Crypto was taking off, all the SPACs (special purpose acquisition companies). Everything was happening. Robinhood and Coinbase were IPO-ing in the middle of 2021. I was trading all day long because there was just so much time.

Trading in 2021 was very different from when I started. The rise of social media, the influencer economy. People and their ideas drove investments — the biggest example of that was GameStop. People believed in one guy with a random username so much that they really changed the financial industry as we knew it.

So I was inspired to think about, How do we productize that? How do we make it simple to follow someone’s trades or investments that you believe in? And that led to the birth of Dub, the platform that makes it simple to copy someone else’s portfolio. That was five years ago. I left school and moved to New York City, and I’ve been working on Dub since.

When it came to fundraising for Dub, I feel like the Harvard dropout piece helped. And I’d sold a company before in high school. The investors from my first company didn’t even know what I was doing but offered to back the venture. So I definitely had a fundraising advantage many people starting out don’t necessarily have. And Dub was lucky to attract some of the best investors in the world — a lot of people that I’d idolized, like the CEOs and founders of Uber, Airbnb, Robinhood, Kalshi. Today, they remain some of my closest mentors.

We did our Series A last year, more than $30 million. As we’ve grown, the money’s been more a function of validation of the business and less that original vision and pitch, because we’re just a much larger and scaled company now. So I would say the fundraising was harder in a sense because it was based on the proof of the business.

It took about two and a half years to build Dub into a product people could use. No one had ever done what we’re doing with copy trading in the U.S. And to be a brokerage like Robinhood or Schwab, you have to get regulated by FINRA, the SEC. So it took us a long time to get that regulatory structure together, and then a long time to get it approved by the regulators. But that gave us a moat because we’re the first ones to do something that no one had really tried before. So that was exciting. Also, this is pre-AI, so building a whole brokerage from the ground up is a lot of work.

You can think of Dub like eBay or Airbnb. Anyone can become a seller. So if they think they have a good strategy or good skill at investing, they can open an account just like a regular user, and they can choose then to publish their portfolio that they build. And a portfolio is like a fund, a basket of stocks they can trade in and out. Once these are launched, any user on Dub can see it, and they can decide to copy that portfolio. Whenever that portfolio trades, it automatically mirrors those trades in any customer account. Now, we have 400 to 500 of these people who have built these portfolios and launched them. It’s a minimum bar of $10,000 to invest in your own portfolio to launch it. So we have some quality filters. And there’s a very diverse range of investing strategies.

We also have 20 premium creators, and it’s a very high bar to become one. You need to have an extended track record. Any creator on Dub has the chance to get “promoted” from a regular creator to a premium creator. They need to meet a minimum time on platform, show that they can beat the market in performance and pass a series of interviews with our investments team so that we know they are real investors worth following and also not just lucky.

Only premium creators get a cut. Premium creators can charge a percentage of assets management fee, similar to ETFs or mutual funds.

Dub makes money through our subscription, which is $89.99 per year, and we also take a cut of the management fees that premium creators make.

We just launched Arlo, one of the industry’s first AI investing assistants that uses algorithms to mirror how financial advisors make decisions. Usually, to hire an investment advisor or put your money at Goldman Sachs, you need to be worth millions, if not tens of millions of dollars. With AI, for the very first time, it’s going to be like when Robinhood made trading free. There’s going to be a democratization event where probably 90% to 95% of the advice that you get from a real-life investment advisor can now be provided by AI.

So we decided to embark on this journey about a year ago, and it’s a lot harder than it looks. It’s not just like talking to ChatGPT or Claude. There’s a lot of work to make sure it gives accurate, regulated advice, no hallucination, but also has the right math and algorithms to figure out accurate mathematical advice to give someone. And it needs to give the same response every time.

I think this will be a really cool moment in history where we look back upon this maybe five to 10 years later, like, Wow, now anyone with a phone can much better manage their money and not go into investing blind. The AI advisor will automatically build you a portfolio: These are the five people that you copy, this is what percentage you should do in each person, etc. And that’s how you build the most optimized, diversified portfolio that is aligned with how you want to invest and your risk tolerance.

We are clearly undergoing one of the most drastic moments in human history. Intelligence in many ways is getting rewritten by a potentially uncontrollable entity. So yes, there’s doom-ism, but on the flip side, optimistically, people at a younger age have never been able to build more with less. I would have loved to have AI when I started Dub. It would have been a whole different company-building experience. So to any young person, I’d say, if you have a dream, go pursue it. It’s one of the most beautiful things in life. Don’t hesitate. You may not have this chance again in a long time.

#5385. XRP Price Could Hit $10,000? From 21Shares’ Forecast to Influencers’ Moonshots

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

XRP price predictions are stretching from Wall Street’s $2.69 bull case to Jake Claver’s extraordinary $10,000 target, as institutional adoption and crypto’s biggest moonshot forecasts collide.

Asset manager 21Shares sees XRP reaching $2.69 in its optimistic 2026 scenario, while veteran trader Peter Brandt has outlined a longer-term $5.40 target. Standard Chartered’s longer-range forecast reaches $28 by 2030, but XRP’s most aggressive supporters are aiming much higher.

Claver continues to stand by his $10,000 XRP price prediction. The forecast would put XRP’s valuation above the combined value of today’s largest financial markets, turning a bullish debate into one of crypto’s most extreme price calls.

21Shares’ January outlook gave XRP a $2.45 base case for 2026, alongside a $2.69 bullish scenario and a $1.60 bearish outcome. The asset manager tied its bullish case to institutional demand, spot XRP ETF inflows, tokenized real-world assets and growing adoption of Ripple’s financial infrastructure.

Peter Brandt’s $5.40 target comes from a longer-term chart pattern that he believes could eventually push XRP beyond its previous record. Standard Chartered has taken the institutional forecast further, projecting XRP at $28 by 2030 as tokenization and stablecoin adoption expand.

EGRAG Crypto has also outlined a $50 scenario based on historical monthly price patterns. This target would give XRP a market capitalization of roughly $3.15 trillion, assuming around 63 billion tokens circulate.

The forecasts become dramatically more ambitious with Claver. The XRP advocate believes the token could first reach $50 to $100 as banks adopt it as a financial asset. He then expects institutional demand and what he calls a systemic repricing to push XRP toward $10,000.

Claver has previously made a $100 prediction for the end of 2025, a target XRP did not reach. His latest forecast nevertheless keeps the five-figure scenario in view.

XRP’s institutional narrative also highlights a question Bitcoin maximalists have debated for years: can Bitcoin become more than a store of value without sacrificing its core security model? Bitcoin Hyper is positioning itself around this opportunity, building a Bitcoin Layer 2 designed to bring faster transactions and smart-contract functionality to the world’s largest cryptocurrency.

The project combines Bitcoin settlement with Solana Virtual Machine execution, aiming to support applications that Bitcoin’s base layer was not designed to handle directly.

Did somebody order a little extra Bitcoin utility? 👀⚡️https://t.co/VNG0P4FWNQ pic.twitter.com/bQAMiOcdUD

Its HYPER token is currently offered through a presale, with a listing price at just $0.0137 and staking rewards offered at 35% APY. The presale has attracted more than $33 million, showing substantial early investor interest.

That combination of a low entry price, staking incentives, and a Bitcoin-native narrative has helped draw attention from crypto investors looking for infrastructure plays beyond established large-cap assets.

The institutional angle is straightforward: if financial firms increasingly use blockchain networks for settlement, tokenization, and programmable finance, Bitcoin’s ecosystem needs infrastructure capable of supporting those activities.

XRP has spent years building its case around payments and institutional liquidity. Bitcoin Hyper is betting that Bitcoin can attract similar infrastructure demand without asking Bitcoin holders to abandon the network they already trust.

#5384. Tech stocks are suffering their biggest selloff since Covid, as investors see premature end to AI datacenter boom

It may have been Blue Tsunami on Tuesday but it was a sea of red that washed over tech stocks on Thursday, covering everything from chips and datacenter companies to software and gig economy firms, as investors panicked that the U.S. midterm election results will bring the AI boom to a premature halt, or at least, a significant slowdown.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq was down more than 1,340 points, or 5.2% in midday trading, shedding more than $3 trillion in market cap, and representing its biggest daily drop since the Liberation Day tariff announcement in April 2025, according to Bloomberg data. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Sector index, which tracks the 30 largest companies in the chips business, was down more than 1,000 points—on track for its single biggest day loss since March 2020.

Some of the biggest names in tech took it on the chin, with Facebook parent company Meta down 3.4%, Microsoft down 2.8%, and Nvidia down 8%.

Thursday’s selloff dragged down the entire market, marking a sharp reversal from Wednesday, when shares rallied following the Democrats’ retaking of the Senate and House of Representatives in the midterm elections. Voters overwhelmingly approved candidates and ballot measures that sought to curtail the buildout of AI data centers in the U.S.

That reality seems to have hit tech stock investors more forcefully on Thursday, as some early signs of the changing business conditions came into focus.

Meta President Dina Powell McCormick, speaking at a conference organized by the Wall Street Journal on Wednesday, acknowledged the new hurdles. Building data centers in the U.S. is “going to be harder,” she said. “I can also tell you that every hyperscaler is now thinking about ‘Do we need to build outside the United States?’ Because they’re enormous investments, hedging those investments is a wise thing to do.”

Dan Ives, the usually bullish analyst at Yorkville Ives, wrote in a note to investors Thursday that he now expects the tech industry’s capex growth to peak next year, instead of in 2028 or 2029.

That capex spree has been an engine of the U.S. economy over the past two years as companies such as Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle, as well as new so-called neocloud companies, raced to build data centers to run AI services. The companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars for the chips, computers, and networking gear, in addition to land, energy, and construction, to erect the data centers.

“While Big Tech and hyperscaler capex should still easily exceed $1 trillion in 2027 the growth rate into 2028 will clearly moderate significantly as the data center buildout comes at a much slower pace given the political map especially in the state of Texas,” Ives wrote.

“We estimate on the low end 10% of the planned 800-1,000 AI focused data centers in the US will now be wiped off the roadmap, with potentially up to 20% of these facing a much longer regulatory road that could further impact the capacity buildout in the US over the next few years,” Ives wrote.

Chip stocks were some of the worst hit, with Micron, the one of the world’s top 3 makers of memory chips, down roughly 14% and AMD, a rival to Nvidia, also down 14%.

Simeon Wallis, chief investment officer at Aprio Wealth Management, told Fortune that uncertainty around data center expansion in Texas, Georgia, and Ohio is leading to worries about AI industry growth. “We see that uncertainty reflected disproportionately in semiconductors, an industry that has been a major beneficiary of AI infrastructure investment,” said Wallis, whose firm manages $6.1 billion in assets.

Neocloud companies, which have taken on large amounts of debt to build data centers that compete with the likes of Amazon and Google, were particularly hard hit as well. Coreweave, one of the leading neocloud companies, was down 9% on Thursday, and on track for an 18% decline over the past two days.

By contrast, Google, one of the industry’s largest cloud  providers, with a search advertising business powering its business, was down a more modest 1.6% on Thursday.

The turmoil triggered by data center worries spread across the broader tech sector throughout Thursday. Software stocks like Salesforce and Snowflake were down 3.6% and 6.4% respectively. Figma, a maker of design software which reported stronger than expected Q3 revenue on Wednesday, was down 17%.

Even gig economy and streaming media companies like DoorDash, Uber, Spotify, and Netflix were all down by multiple percentage points by the time the market closed Thursday.

“Ultimately, we believe that markets can over-react in the short term to speculating who future winners and losers are,” said Wallis, of Aprio Wealth Management.

With additional reporting by Scott DeCarlo and Catherina Gioino.

Alexei Oreskovic is the Tech editor at Fortune.
