#5338. China’s Largest Startup Deal Ever Lifts Global Venture Funding To $59B In October

Global venture funding in October totaled $59 billion, a 45% jump from a year earlier, per Crunchbase data, in large part due to a record-setting deal for China’s DeepSeek. The company’s $15.9 billion funding round marked the largest-ever venture deal for a Chinese company ever, and came in the same month that two other frontier labs raised blockbuster Series A rounds totaling at or close to $1 billion.

The bulk of October’s venture funding was invested in the two leading countries for startup investment, with companies based in the U.S. and China raising $28 billion and $20.6 billion last month, respectively. The last time more than $20 billion was invested in China in a single month was June 2018, when Ant Group raised $14 billion in its Series C funding.

Funding concentrated in seven companies that raised billion-dollar rounds, accounting for just over 40% of October’s venture funding. These large amounts were invested in frontier labs, manufacturing, energy, semiconductors, prediction markets and spend management software. Private equity led much of this funding, along with a few multistage venture firms including Sequoia Capital, Index Ventures and Lux Capital.

DeepSeek’s $15.9 billion raise at a valuation of $90 billion marked the largest private funding by a Chinese tech company on record. The deal places DeepSeek among the Top 10 most highly funded private companies. It also makes it the second most highly valued Chinese company after ByteDance, and the third most highly valued private frontier lab after U.S. companies Anthropic and OpenAI.

DeepSeek wasn’t the only Chinese frontier lab to raise big in October. Moonshot AI, a rival open-source lab, reportedly reached a $50 billion value in October, making it the 11th most valuable private company on The Crunchbase Unicorn Board. The startup has also reportedly confidentially filed to go public on the Hong Kong stock exchange.

Massachusetts-based manufacturing startup Re:Build raised the second-largest funding deal last month, a $2.1 billion round. The company partners with industrial companies and innovators from the product design phase to large-scale production and says it has 2.4 million square feet of manufacturing capacity.

Other large rounds last month went to Axiom, which raised $2 billion for power and grid capacity build out for data centers; spend-management platform Ramp, which raised $1.85 billion and said its ARR has reached $2 billion; open-source semiconductor company Tenstorrent, which says it  raised a $1.5 billion Series E funding and recently moved its  headquarters to Silicon Valley from Canada; prediction market Kalshi, which raised a $1 billion Series E; and frontier lab Flapping Airplanes, which raised a $1 billion Series A.

A further eight companies raised rounds north of $500 million last month. They spanned industries ranging from frontier labs, robotics, legal and chips, to agentic AI and healthcare. Among the most notable was TypeSafe AI, which says it raised an $870 million Series A funding on the heels of rapid developer adoption of its decision model Jev.

A total of 66% of global funding was in AI-driven companies in October, with semiconductor companies gaining market share this past month.

The U.S. IPO market was slow in anticipation of Anthropic’s November IPO. The offering could surpass even SpaceX’s record-setting June listing that raised $85.7 billion.

On the M&A front, at least nine venture-backed companies were acquired for more than $1 billion last month, including Uber’s acquisition of 19-year-old ezCater for $2.3 billion.

With two months remaining, 2026 has already set records for acquisitions, IPOs and funding rounds across major venture markets. October extended that momentum, but also highlighted how concentrated this cycle has become: Seven companies accounted for more than 40% of global funding, while AI-driven businesses captured two-thirds.

The question heading into year-end is how widely that momentum will spread, as Anthropic prepares to list in what could be the largest IPO of all time.

#5337. 1.8 Billion XRP Moves in Just 24 Hours as XRP Ledger Shows Signs of Recovery

The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. A headline claiming that 1.8 billion XRP moved across the XRP Ledger within 24 hours has revived discussion of a network recovery. The figure hasn't been independently verified for a dated 24-hour period, so treat it as a reported claim, not confirmed evidence of a new trend.

The XRP Ledger handles payments, decentralized exchange transactions and tokenized assets. Payment volumes reflects the network activity, but the number needs context. Large transfers can be exchange custody movements, internal treasury operations or transfers between wallets controlled by the same entity.

None of that necessarily signals fresh investor demand or new capital entering the market.

Recent verified reporting shows why the distinction matters. One October snapshot had daily payment volume jumping to about 137.7 million XRP, still below its 30-day average of roughly 496 million.

Another October reading, around 363.3 million XRP, came with the same caution: a one-day rise did not establish a sustained recovery.

A reading near 1.8 billion XRP usually comes at the end of the week where most of the network activity occurs. The most likely outcome is always the same: high activity by Thursday and Friday and a tubmling on the weekend, with a recovery starting on Monday.

Other indicators help separate real adoption from a passing spike: active addresses, successful payment counts, decentralized-exchange trading, liquidity and how transaction sizes are distributed. Even high transaction counts can mislead when automated activity dominates, as recent investigations into small-value stablecoin payments on XRPL showed.

Network usage and XRP's market price are only indirectly related. More settlement activity doesn't guarantee higher token prices, and speculative buying can lift prices with no matching improvement in usage. Broader market conditions and exchange liquidity matter too.

A verified natural burst of XRP movement could mean renewed engagement with the network. A more convincing signal would be several consecutive days of stronger, widely distributed activity, backed by improving liquidity and sustained user demand, which rarely happens.

#5335. Most Venture Capital Is Going To Companies That Are Founded Or Led By Billionaires

The majority of U.S. venture capital nowadays goes to companies founded or led by men who are already billionaires.

This is not a difficult stat to unearth. So far this year, just seven companies raised more than half of all seed- through growth-stage investment. They’re mostly familiar names: OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI (now part of SpaceX), Anduril Industries, Databricks, Prometheus and The Boring Co.

These companies raised more than $260 billion in equity funding in the first 10 months of the year. That’s just over 50% of the U.S. seed and venture investment over the same period, per Crunchbase data.

Founders and CEOs of these seven companies are also well-known — and exceptionally  well-off to boot.

Two founders are particularly famous. They are the world’s wealthiest men: Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos.

Musk founded xAI and The Boring Co., and also co-founded OpenAI, (though he has no known equity stake in the latter). And while outside investors funded these companies, Musk could have also afforded to do so himself.

Ditto for Bezos, who in 2025 launched the physical AI startup Prometheus, which raised $12 billion earlier this year. Bezos’ own net worth, meanwhile, is calculated at more than $350 billion.

The two highest valuation startups — OpenAI and the soon-to-be-public Anthropic — also have prominent billionaire founders and CEOs. However, they have mixed backstories to their wealth.

OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman primarily made his vast wealth through investments in Y Combinator startups, including Stripe and Reddit. Altman has said he does not have an equity stake in OpenAI beyond a sliver from an old YC round. Co-founder Greg Brockman, by contrast, has a larger stake in OpenAI that was reportedly valued around $30 billion earlier this year.

At Anthropic, meanwhile, all seven company co-founders have similar-sized equity stakes, and each is worth billions. This includes the AI giant’s most famous co-founder, CEO Dario Amodei.

Databricks and Anduril, meanwhile, both have founders serving as CEOs who have amassed billion-dollar-plus net worths during their tenures.

Databricks co-founder and CEO Ali Ghodsi has a reported $7.6 billion net worth, with the company he leads valued at around $190 billion following an August financing.

Anduril co-founder and CEO Brian Schimpf, meanwhile, has an estimated $1.5 billion net worth as a result of his stake in the $61 billion valuation defense industry disruptor. Co-founder Palmer Luckey, who sold his virtual reality startup Oculus to Meta for $2 billion in 2014 before starting Anduril, has an estimated $5.9 billion net worth.

Several other founders and CEOs of startups that raised some of this year’s largest rounds are billionaires too. This includes Wonder founder Marc Lore, Figure founder Brett Adcock, and Surge AI founder and CEO Edwin Chen, among others.

We can split the billionaires who founded this year’s most heavily funded startups into two broad subcategories. There are those who became billionaires through the startup that just raised capital. And there are those who were already billionaires through prior companies or investments.

Ghodsi, Amodei and Brockman fit in the first group. In the second group, of course, we can put Musk and Bezos, as well as Altman and Luckey, who became a 21-year-old billionaire following the Oculus sale.

Historically, neither billionaire type was a particularly common recipient of venture funding rounds. The term “unicorn” as a moniker for private companies valued at $1 billion or more only entered the lexicon in 2013, when this asset class became noticeably large. In prior decades, founders and CEOs mostly only hit billionaire status after their startups went public or sold in high-priced acquisitions.

But times change. And in tandem, our image of what a startup funding recipient looks like should evolve as well.

True, quite a bit of capital still flows to the stereotypical venture recipients: first-time founders or serial entrepreneurs whose prior companies didn’t make them fabulously wealthy. But a majority of venture funding now does not go to these classic startup types.

Instead, it goes to companies with valuations already high enough to warrant billionaire status for their stakeholders as well as ventures founded by men who are already billionaires.

In late October 2026, Zcash (ZEC) reached a key milestone: the coin's price consolidated around $1,280, and its market capitalization hit $21.8 billion. However, the rapid rally was overshadowed by a sharp split within the community.

The trigger of the crisis was not a technical problem but a revolt of large investors over the targeted spending of capital.

Zcash Community Grants (ZCG), the organization that distributes part of the miners' block reward, launched the Zcash Adoption Pool program. The fund directed grants toward the integration of vulnerable groups like refugees without access to banks.

The decision sparked protest from major players, since ZCG's charter allows it to distribute multimillion-dollar budgets bypassing the coinholder vote. The "whale" revolt moved into the practical realm: a major holder under the pseudonym "big z" publicly announced a full sell-off of his ZEC holdings.

According to him, the fund should finance cryptography, not political manifestos.

The local conflict quickly grew into a debate about the nature of decentralized money, which industry heavyweights joined. Developer Sean Bowe published a manifesto on the future of ZCG, in which he called for revising the fund's financing due to the anomalous surge in the ZEC price.

The initiative was unexpectedly supported by legendary investor Naval Ravikant, who laconically snapped that a $50 million cap is more than enough for community grants.

Meanwhile, the fund's activists continue to insist that private money is a "humanitarian imperative" and a public good.

However, Gemini exchange co-founder Tyler Winklevoss harshly challenged this thesis: a commercial network with transaction fees cannot be a public good. Winklevoss compared ZCG's actions to "taxation without representation" and called for leaving the development of Zcash to the free market.

The pressure on the price from the whales' coin sell-off coincided with the launch of direct ZEC deposits on the decentralized Rujira Network on October 29.

After failing to break above $1,390, the price settled in the $1,220–1,245 $range, still well below the all-time high of $1,698 set in late September. The fundamental dispute over who should control Zcash's millions remains open.

#5331. The Crunchbase Tech Layoffs Tracker

The past week has seen at least a dozen companies from both overseas and the U.S. reporting tech layoffs.

Leading by the count of workers affected is New South Wales, Australia-based Canva, an online design and visual communications platform. According to an update posted on its website, the company is reducing its global workforce by 22%, or 1,271 people. With workers based in Austin and San Francisco, it is unclear how many of those layoffs will affect U.S. employees.

Amazon rejoins the tracker this week with a pair of reported layoffs. The first involves 250 workers in its devices and services division, a cutback that took place last week, and another 95 employees in positions including software engineers, product managers and operations employees. According to a report in TheStreet, the affected workers are scheduled to be laid off between Dec. 7 and Jan. 25.

According to a report in the Sacramento Business Journal, Santa Clara, California-based Intel has laid off 67 workers from its Folsom, California, location.

In the lone shutdown reported this week, Ollie AI, a subscription-based AI assistant, will officially close the app on Nov. 6. According to a report in TechCrunch, Bill Lennon, the San Diego-based company’s co-founder and CEO, cited the pressures of the burgeoning AI industry, saying “We got close, but ultimately couldn’t keep up.”

The following companies were added to the tracker this week:

Layoffs during the weeks ended Nov. 4, 2026: At least 2,982 U.S. tech sector employees were laid off or scheduled for layoffs, per a Crunchbase News tally.

In 2025: Around 127,000 workers were let go from U.S.-based tech companies according to our tally.

In 2024: At least 95,667 workers at U.S.-based tech companies lost their jobs in 2024, according to a Crunchbase News tally.

In 2023: More than 191,000 workers in U.S.-based tech companies (or tech companies with a large U.S. workforce) were laid off in mass job cuts.

In 2022: More than 93,000 jobs were slashed from public and private tech companies in the U.S.

This tracker includes layoffs conducted by U.S.-based companies or those with a strong U.S. presence and is updated at least bi-weekly. We’ve included both startups and publicly traded, tech-heavy companies. We’ve also included companies based elsewhere that have a sizable team in the United States, such as Klarna, even when it’s unclear how much of the U.S. workforce has been affected by layoffs.

Layoff and workforce figures are best estimates based on reporting. We source the layoffs from media reports, our own reporting, social media posts and layoffs.fyi, a crowdsourced database of tech layoffs.

We recently updated our layoffs tracker to reflect the most recent round of layoffs each company has conducted. This allows us to quickly and more accurately track layoff trends, which is why you might notice some changes in our most recent numbers.

If an employee headcount cannot be confirmed to our standards, we note it as “unclear.”

A layoff can be either a permanent termination of someone’s employment — usually for cost-saving reasons — or a temporary one because there’s not enough work to justify a full workforce. Tech company layoffs generally fall into the permanent category.

A mass layoff is when a significant number of a company’s employees are cut in a short period of time, often as a result of economic conditions.

Tech layoffs started to surge in 2022 and continued in 2023 and 2024. Companies have given various reasons for conducting layoffs.

Some companies — especially those in the e-commerce sector — nearly doubled their employee headcount to meet consumer demand during the COVID-19 pandemic’s stay-at-home mandates, and later found that they were overstaffed as daily life returned to normal.

Large tech employers such as Salesforce and Google parent Alphabet noted that their post-pandemic layoffs followed several years of rapid hiring fueled by fast growth — between 2019 and 2022, some companies nearly doubled their employee headcount. Some large tech companies also cited slowing sales and fears of a recession as reasons for downsizing.

Venture-backed startups, meanwhile, also cut jobs as a way to cut costs and preserve their cash reserves, as venture funding fell significantly after the peak in 2021. Some startups that ran out of cash and couldn’t raise new funding found themselves filing for bankruptcy or shutting down.

Intel Corp. laid off the largest number of people among U.S. tech employers in 2024, by our count. The semiconductor giant laid off more than 15,000 employees last year.

It was followed closely by electric-car maker Tesla, which cut more than 14,000 roles, and networking company Cisco, with more than 10,000 total roles cut.

In 2023, Amazon layoffs led the numbers with 16,000 roles cut. Layoffs at Alphabet, the parent company of Google, totaled about 12,000, and Microsoft’s layoffs totaled about 10,000 workers in 2023, as did Facebook parent Meta’s layoffs.

Many venture-backed tech startups have also done layoffs as venture capital investment has fallen sharply since the peak in 2021, and falling startup valuations factor into their decisions to conduct layoffs.

Yes, more layoffs are likely coming. While there are signs that the volume of layoffs is tapering, experts we talked to expect job cuts in the tech sector to continue for the foreseeable future as large tech companies and startups continue to battle economic headwinds.

Seed and early-stage startups in particular may continue to conduct layoffs in an attempt to extend their cash runways in a difficult venture funding environment.

Tech layoffs noticeably increased at the start of 2022, ramped up in 2023, waned somewhat in 2024 and have continued in 2025.

Signs that may indicate a company is more likely to conduct layoffs include:

Layoffs declined in 2024 compared to the previous year, but are expected to continue into 2025, although likely not at the level seen in 2023. Startups that need to preserve cash to extend their runways are more likely to conduct layoffs.

Tech layoffs will likely slow when venture capital funding increases and the startup economy stabilizes, as well as when market conditions improve and more startups gain liquidity via IPOs.

Startups that raised capital during the venture funding heyday at inflated valuations in 2021 are more likely to need to conduct layoffs if they’re not able to sustain their previous valuations or growth projections.

Tech layoffs started surging in the 2022 market correction, with an estimated 93,000 U.S. tech workers laid off that year. That figure more than doubled in 2023, with around 200,000 U.S. tech employees laid off, according to our Tech Layoffs Tracker. Layoffs abated again in 2024, with around 95,000 reported tech layoffs.

Keep in mind, many companies don’t report detailed layoffs figures, and some companies continue hiring after cuts for positions deemed more beneficial to the business.

No, according to experts in the sector, who say a sale is unlikely to solve a tech company’s cash-flow issues.

This is especially true as fewer startup M&A deals are happening in the current downturn.

Tech layoffs have hit across departments at many companies.

Many layoffs from the large tech giants were software engineers. Startups tend to be more likely to retain engineers in favor of doing layoffs in their talent and recruiting, marketing and other departments.

Google cut roles in its sales, recruiting, product and engineering teams. Amazon layoffs included jobs in its AWS cloud unit, at its social video platform Twitch, and in its advertising department. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the company’s recruiting department would be the first to see job cuts.

October ended for XRP with a drop of almost 19%. The main blow was the $6.3 billion hack of the Binance exchange, which dragged down the entire market. However, the sell-off recorded at the lows activated large buy orders — the current liquidity map points to the formation of local support.

Now the XRP price is squeezed in a narrow corridor around $1.25, testing the boundaries of the local bottom.

CoinGlass derivatives market data shows that the asset has literally been pinned to the floor. At the current rate of $1.2505, the critical level of long liquidations is at the $1.2292 mark. The probability of its test within 24 hours is 54%. From above, the price is held back by a block of short sellers at the $1.4292 level.

At the same time, the market has already been cleared of excessive leverage — $37.6 million in longs were forcibly closed in October.

The TradingView technical picture confirms the importance of the current line. On the weekly chart, XRP is trading right on the key 200-week moving average ($1.25–$1.28) — this is a powerful historical level from which the vertical takeoff began in August. The daily oscillator dropped to the 36.85 mark.

Historically, reaching this oversold zone has always preceded an upward trend reversal.

Additional pressure was exerted by the results of the Ripple Swell conference. The new RLUSD stablecoin takes over the company’s institutional products (including custodial services for Coinbase and Robinhood), which temporarily reduced direct demand for XRP.

Against this background, the assets of U.S. XRP ETFs corrected to $1.42–$1.47 billion solely due to the drop in the price of the token itself, while inflows into the funds froze near zero.

The $1.20–$1.25 range remains the main foundation. The fact that the dump on the Binance news was instantly bought back proves the strength of buyers. If they hold the $1.2292 line and return the price above the daily average at $1.3145, the current marks will become the official bottom.

Conversely, a breakdown of $1.20 will open the way to the August lows around $0.98–$1.00.

#5329. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

The volume of tokenized stocks on the Ethereum network grew by 170% over the year, reaching $827 million by the end of October 2026. According to a fresh report from the analytics platform Token Terminal, the real-world assets (RWA) sector has outgrown the experimental stage.

While the total value of tokenized securities on alternative chains is measured in billions of dollars, the volume on Ethereum remains in the range from $827 million to $841 million, and the network remains one of the key channels for digitized equities.

The rapid growth of the sector is largely tied to how the digital assets themselves are structured. At the moment, 86% of tokenized stocks are issued under the model of classic stablecoins: the instruments are fully backed by the underlying asset in a 1:1 ratio and, at the same time, function without the direct operational or legal participation of the issuer of the original securities.

Ethereum, which currently controls 53.8% of the global stablecoin market ($158.71 billion out of a total of $294.75 billion), carries its well-tested and liquid infrastructure over to traditional securities.

Professional market participants assess this shift as a potential repetition of the success of stablecoins, but this time in the stock market.

While spot infrastructure is being built on Ethereum, a completely different, speculative life is unfolding in the derivatives market. Here, historical records are being set on decentralized venues: open interest, with contracts on the same tokenized stocks accounting for the largest share, has reached $1.76 billion.

An example of this ecosystem is the Hyperliquid platform, whose native token HYPE is trading at around $87.70. The coin is supported by an inflow of new holders, as well as automated tokenomics: the platform directs $1.24 million daily to buying back HYPE from the open market.

Representatives of the investment community have outlined the zone from $70 to $76 as a key long-term support level. Current market conditions point to a possible move toward the $90–$100 range.

The existence of this parallel reality — from spot on Ethereum to highly liquid futures on Hyperliquid — shows that the blockchain is becoming a multi-level environment for different types of capital.

#5327. Crunchbase Data: Less Than 2% Of 2026 Venture Funding Went To Post-Election Red States

For the past few decades, the vast majority of U.S. startup funding has consistently gone to companies in blue states or purple states, where Democrats control all or some statewide offices.

But with Tuesday’s election results, the investment divide between blue, purple and red states has grown even more pronounced.

So far this year, less than 2% of all startup investment has gone to companies in post-election red states, defined as those that will have both a Republican governor and two Republican U.S. senators.

The red states’ share is much smaller than in years past due to five states shifting to purple. Of those, the largest venture hub is Texas, which shifted to purple with the election of Democratic Senator James Talarico and Governor Gina Hinojosa, followed by Ohio.

This year, as of Election Day, startups in the remaining 17 red states 1, which are home to nearly a quarter of Americans, had collectively pulled in just $8.6 billion in venture funding, with Florida, Tennessee and Utah among the largest contributors. To put that in perspective: It’s less than the typical nationwide total in a single week.

The 10 purple U.S. states2, meanwhile, are home to just over a quarter of Americans and pulled in about $28.6 billion this year as of Election Day. That’s much higher than the red state tally, but still less than 6% of all U.S. startup funding.

Beyond the aforementioned newcomers Texas and Ohio, several other purple states regularly pull in sizable venture funding, including Pennsylvania, North Carolina and to some extent Wisconsin.

Also worth noting: The divide between red, purple and blue states is somewhat less stark when it comes to round counts. About 12% of startup financings of $1 million or more went to purple state companies this year, and about 9% went to red states.

Broadly, it looks like backers are still finding plenty of investment-worthy talent outside of blue states when it comes to smaller deals. However, they are concentrating most of their capital into big AI rounds for California and New York companies.

This brings us to our next point: Blue states receive the overwhelming majority of startup funding, of which most goes to California.3 Per a Crunchbase analysis last week, California companies had pulled in more than three-fourths of all U.S. startup funding in 2026. Most of that stems from mega-financings for San Francisco-based OpenAI and Anthropic. While no other state comes close to California for attracting investment, the nearest runners up are also predominantly blue states, including New York and Massachusetts. In total, blue states have pulled in a staggering $481 billion in startup investment this year as of Election Day, per Crunchbase data, a new record. Politics and what makes for a venture hub So is it politics, or coincidence? Broadly speaking, the qualities that geographic startup hubs share — such as a deep tech talent pool, urban environs, leading tech companies and top research universities — aren’t specifically the domain of blue states. That said, predominantly rural states, which tend to lean red, are less likely to have those ingredients. Even so, there’s no rule against red state startup prowess. Austin, for example, managed to cement its status as a major tech hub even while Texas remained solidly under Republican control. And Utah also boasts a sophisticated startup scene. But following a Democratic electoral sweep, it’s hardly a surprise that more startup hubs now find themselves located in blue or purple states. Something potentially enormous could be approaching for Tesla (TSLA) by January 1, 2027. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI predicts that TSLA stock could be a standout performer through Q4 and into 2027, based on a hypothetical landmark catalyst that isn’t impossible.

The concept focuses on Tesla obtaining widespread regulatory approval for unsupervised full self-driving robotaxi operations in several major markets, while also scaling up the production and deployment of Optimus humanoid robots beyond current expectations.

In this scenario, Tesla would quickly shift from primarily an electric vehicle manufacturer to a high-margin platform company centered on autonomy and robotics. This transformation could open up multi-trillion-dollar markets and significantly increase the company’s stock valuation.

On the higher timeframes, TSLA has been consolidating in the $390–$415 region after a recovery from lower levels earlier in the year. Price continues to hold above key intermediate supports while facing resistance around the $420–$450 zone.

In a standard bull market for growth and technology stocks, a sustained breakout above $480–$520 would confirm intermediate strength and open the path to higher-cycle targets.

Under the extreme robotaxi approval and Optimus scaling scenario outlined above, clearing significant resistance levels would likely trigger powerful measured-move extensions and multi-cycle projections from the longer-term base.

Momentum indicators currently sit in neutral-to-constructive territory with substantial room to run into the strong overbought readings typical of high-beta technology rallies.

Key nearer-term supports sit near $380–$390 and $350–$360; holding those levels would keep the broader recovery structure intact.

Tesla may open Optimus reservations in December.Investor Modar Alaoui says Tesla told him so.They'd launch with his Humanoids Summit, Dec 1–2.Optimus V3 is set to be demoed there.Musk expects deliveries to other companies around end of 2027. pic.twitter.com/b2H2qEcl0w

In recent weeks, Tesla has delivered several updates that support longer-term optimism around autonomy and robotics. In its Q3 2026 results, the company beat adjusted EPS estimates and generated positive free cash flow, even as it ramped spending on AI and future products.

More importantly, Tesla confirmed that production of Optimus humanoid robots has begun on high-volume lines in Fremont, marking a shift from prototypes to early manufacturing.

On the autonomy side, the Cybercab robotaxi service continues to expand, with the Austin fleet growing rapidly, plans to launch in Dallas, and an ambition to deliver the first Cybercabs to customers by the end of 2026.

Unsupervised robotaxi miles have increased sharply, while Full Self-Driving subscriptions remain on a strong upward trajectory. Tesla has also entered volume production of the Semi.

While near-term profits remain under pressure from heavy investment, these operational milestones reinforce the narrative of Tesla evolving beyond vehicles into high-margin autonomy and robotics platforms.

Under this highly speculative scenario, and assuming supportive market conditions return, Tesla (TSLA) could reach between $1,800 and $3,000, with a stretch target toward $4,500+ by January 1, 2027.

This remains pure speculation and entertainment, not a realistic base-case outlook. The catalyst would require extraordinary regulatory progress and execution on robotaxi and Optimus at a scale that is currently highly unlikely.

#5324. Sector Snapshot: Construction Robotics Funding Soars To $1.6B, Tripling Previous Peak

Construction companies are struggling to find enough workers. For startups, that means venture investors are pouring money into companies betting that robots can help close the gap.

Companies spanning construction and robotics have raised about $1.6 billion this year through Oct. 29 — more than 4x the $389 million recorded in all of 2025 — according to Crunchbase data. The surge was driven by three companies that raised the majority of the funding.

The broad trend: For contractors struggling to hire, the appeal of construction-oriented tech offerings is straightforward: They need to get work done and there aren’t enough skilled workers to do it. The AI-driven data center building boom is only adding to that competition for workers. Labor shortages remain the biggest cause of project delays, according to a recent survey by the Associated General Contractors of America and NCCER.

Some of the technology is already at work on job sites.

San Francisco-based Bedrock Robotics, this year’s largest funding recipient in the sector, said in August that excavators equipped with its autonomous systems were operating without human operators on commercial projects in Texas and Nevada.

The numbers: With roughly two months left in the year, funding has already surpassed the previous five years combined.

Companies spanning construction and robotics raised about $1.6 billion through Oct. 29, 3x the previous high of $506 million in 2021, according to our dataset that goes back to 2018. This year’s total is also more than 3x the 2021 high of $506 million.

So far, the funding surge reflects much bigger bets rather than more deals. The sector has recorded 30 rounds this year, compared with 28 in all of 2025. Bedrock alone accounts for $870 million across two deals — more than half of this year’s total. This underscores just how much a few large financings are impacting the recovery.

Austin-based Icon, which builds homes using 3D printing, also raised two rounds in 2026. It has raised nearly $800 million since its 2017 inception. A company spokesperson told Crunchbase News that the company has taken its technology from an experiment to “an in-the-field system that can build faster, with fewer people, less waste, greater design freedom and lower cost.”

To date, the company has built more than 270 homes and structures across five states and two countries. It says that it’s on pace to grow revenue by 4x this year.

“Early on, the question was whether a robotic construction system could build a good home,” the spokesperson wrote via email. “Today, the question is whether a company can deliver at volume, across geographies and project types, and improve its economics with each build. That’s only answerable with time in the field.”

Bedrock Robotics was the largest funding recipient in 2026, impressively raising $870 million across two rounds. The 2-year-old company, which converts existing heavy construction equipment into autonomous machines, announced a $600 million Series C in October led by CapitalG and Emergence Capital. That round, which valued Bedrock at $4.1 billion, followed a $270 million Series B in February led by CapitalG and Valor Atreides AI Fund.

Austin-based construction technology company Icon also raised two rounds, bringing its listed 2026 funding to $265 million. Its largest financing was a $200 million Series D in October led by Baillie Gifford and BlackRock, following a $65 million Series C in March.

Another $200 million round went to Gravis Robotics, based in Zurich, Switzerland, which develops technology to retrofit construction machinery for autonomous earthmoving and excavation. SoftBank led the company’s Series A in August, which valued the startup at $1 billion post-money.

Beyond those large financings, investors backed companies automating homebuilding and specific construction tasks.

London-based All3, which uses AI and robotics to design, manufacture and assemble buildings, raised $25 million in April led by RTP Global. Origin, based in San Francisco, developing a general-purpose construction robot, secured $20 million in October, led by Accel and Zacua Ventures.

Acquisitions have dominated exit activity in construction robotics and related jobsite automation this year.

One of the largest disclosed deals was Carpinteria, California-based Procore’s acquisition of DroneDeploy, a San Francisco-based platform that combines imagery from drones, ground robots and cameras to track construction progress and site conditions. Procore announced the approximately $845 million cash transaction in July and closed it in September.

Other buyers have focused on automating the work itself. In January, Oshkosh subsidiary JLG Industries acquired the core technology developed by Canvas, a San Francisco-based startup known for robotic drywall finishing.

Heavy-equipment autonomy also attracted buyers. In March, HavocAI completed its acquisition of Palo Alto, California-based Teleo, whose technology lets operators remotely oversee heavy machinery.

The following month, San Francisco-based Pronto confirmed that Atoms, Travis Kalanick’s physical AI company, had completed its acquisition for an undisclosed price. Pronto’s autonomous haulage technology now reportedly underpins Atoms’ mining division.

Public offerings have been less prominent, with no known IPOs this year by companies focused specifically on construction robotics. The broader construction technology market did produce a sizable debut: Columbia, Missouri-based EquipmentShare, an equipment rental and connected-jobsite technology company, raised approximately $747 million in gross proceeds in its January IPO, selling 30.5 million shares at $24.50 each.

For all the variety in the companies attracting funding, this year’s surge has so far largely rested on three: Bedrock, Icon and Gravis, which together accounted for more than $1.3 billion, or about 83%, of the roughly $1.6 billion raised. Investors are placing unusually large bets on a small group of companies, even as acquisitions give others a route into larger businesses already serving construction customers.

#5322. Why Coinbase Bitcoin Discount Just Hit a Yearly High

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Classic crypto market metrics have suddenly stopped reflecting reality. Bitcoin’s discount on the U.S. exchange Coinbase relative to the international Binance has hit a yearly high, with the Coinbase Premium Index collapsing to around −0.06%.

In normal times, such a chart gives traders a cold sweat: the index going deep into the red zone means that large funds in the U.S. have started massively dumping crypto.

However, the current collapse of the indicator turned out to be a technical illusion. It was provoked by the emergency freeze of operations on Binance immediately after a large-scale hack of the exchange, which completely blocked classic cross-exchange arbitrage.

The anomalous price gap coincided with the largest incident in the industry’s history: on October 29–30, hackers attacked Binance’s hot wallets, withdrawing about $6.3 billion. The exchange promptly froze half of the stolen funds on the blockchain, and the head of the platform promised to fully cover the remaining client losses from the SAFU reserve fund.

Nevertheless, amid the panic, the price of Bitcoin dropped to $77,000–$78,000.

To localize the problem, Binance completely shut the gateways — it temporarily banned any deposits and withdrawals of funds. This decision instantly paralyzed cross-exchange arbitrage. Large players physically could not buy the temporarily cheaper Bitcoin on Coinbase and transfer it to Binance to even out the price.

Liquidity was locked inside the platforms, which caused the discount to artificially swell to its widest level in a year.

As noted by Galaxy Research’s head of research Alex Thorn, due to the blocking of transactions, the discount on Coinbase temporarily stopped being a signal of weak demand in the U.S.

On November 1, Binance announced a phased reopening of withdrawals, starting with BTC and ETH. Now the market is waiting to see how quickly arbitrageurs eliminate the gap. If the gap closes in the coming days, it means the anomaly was purely technical.

If the negative spread becomes entrenched, it will be an alarming signal of a real cooling of American capital.

Crypto stocks edged higher before Tuesday’s open, November 3, even as Nvidia, Costco and Nike joined the companies blocking tokenized versions of their shares on OKXICE, taking the count to 50, and an AI chip sell-off sent Seoul’s Kospi down 3.6%.

The bounce is small, and it follows a bad month. Coinbase traded at $138.74 at 13:00 UTC, up 0.7% from Monday’s close of $137.83, its lowest finish since February 2024. Robinhood, Strategy and Circle rose between 0.5% and 1.1%, and Galaxy led with 2.8% after losing 8.8% on Monday.

The bigger story for the sector is the pushback against tokenization. Objectors to OKXICE, the 24/7 venue for tokenized US stocks that OKX is building with NYSE owner ICE, went from 16 to 50 in 11 days. Today is the deadline for companies notified on October 4, so the list could still grow, while Coinbase, Robinhood and the other crypto names on it have yet to say no.

Asia offered no lift. After a 1.1% drop in the Nasdaq on Monday, Samsung and SK hynix dragged the Kospi to 5,648.79, Shanghai slipped 0.8%, and Tokyo was shut for a holiday. Only Hong Kong closed higher, and Bitcoin held steady through the session at $77,326.

Investors are DUMPING US tech stocks at a rapid pace:The Nasdaq 100 index has dropped -6.1% over the last 3 trading sessions, its biggest 3-day decline since the April 2025 Liberation Day selloff. $QQQ This also marks the 3rd-largest 3-day decline since the 2022 bear market.… pic.twitter.com/jNvmex3HZj

So why are so many companies saying no to tokenization, and why are markets red from Seoul to New York?

Because they would carry the risk and see little of the benefit. OKXICE, the venue OKX is building with NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange, wants to offer round-the-clock trading of US stocks as tokens, paid for in stablecoins.

Under the SEC’s exemption, a company can keep its shares off such a venue if an outside firm does the tokenizing. It has 30 days from notice to object, and the objections have come fast:

The newest 12 are Nvidia, Costco, Micron, CrowdStrike, Corning, IREN, USA Rare Earth, Bloom Energy, Nike, Palo Alto Networks, Reddit and Hewlett Packard Enterprise. They join Microsoft, Alphabet, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan, which runs its own blockchain unit and says it still likes the technology.

The fight is over shareholder rights, especially votes. “Right now companies like Goldman and Microsoft see all of the risk and none of the upside,” Injective’s COO Mirza Uddin told CNBC.

OKXICE co-chair Andrew Cuomo isn’t backing down. “We are at the very beginning of the rollout of fundamentally different market structure,” he said at the October 30 press conference.

Discover: JPMorgan and Coca-Cola Block Tokenized Stocks on OKXICE as Objectors Hit 33. Coinbase and Robinhood Stay Out of the List

Only the crypto names avoided objection to tokenisation, along with several major US stocks. Coinbase, Robinhood, Circle, Strategy, BitGo and Securitize remain outside the objection list, as do Apple, Amazon, Tesla, SpaceX and Netflix.

One crypto-born company did say no. IREN, the Bitcoin miner that now earns more from renting computers to AI firms than from mining, objected in the latest batch.

Silence isn’t a yes, though. Venues get up to five business days to publish objections, so companies that answered this week may not show up until next week’s notice, and staying off the list doesn’t guarantee a stock will trade at launch.

The AI trade is cracking again. Big Tech results last week showed Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft will keep spending heavily on data centres and chips, and investors want to see faster returns first.

Monday’s selling on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq fell 1.1%, hit Asia’s chipmakers on Tuesday:

Seoul’s slide is the one to watch. The Kospi closed at a record 9,114.55 on June 22 and is now 38% lower, with 17% of that lost since the end of September.

Oil added to the strain. Brent climbed 1.7% to $106.58 after reports of limited US strikes on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz, a day after it fell more than 7% on hopes of new talks.

Hong Kong’s crypto stocks split. Exchange operator OSL rose 0.4%, and Boyaa Interactive, which holds Bitcoin, fell 5.1%.

They have been sold off with tech, then sold again for crypto. Every big name is down at least 12% since the end of September, and the first trading day after the Binance hack was the worst of the run.

Coinbase’s daily chart shows how far the slide has gone. The stock is $34 under its 50-day average and more than $50 under its 200-day, and Monday’s close was the lowest since February 2024.

COIN 1D chart. Source: Yahoo Finance (Nasdaq).

The tokenization fight won’t move share prices on its own. For crypto stocks, today’s pre-market bounce still has to survive Wall Street’s open and a long night of election results.

#5320. Nvidia, Nike and 48 Other Companies Oppose OKX Stock Tokenization Plan

A total of 50 companies, including Nvidia (NVDA) and Nike (NKE), have officially raised objections to the trading of tokenized shares on a new platform backed by crypto exchange OKX and the parent company of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE).

As per the most recent public notice by the joint venture between crypto exchange OKX and Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), OKXICE, the total number of companies objecting to the initiative has reached 50 as of Oct. 30.

The total increased from 38 companies on Oct. 28, with 12 additional companies raising objections in just two days.

The new names that recently raised objections include Nvidia, Nike, Costco (COST), Micron Technology (MU) and Reddit (RDDT).

Other companies that have recently raised objections include cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike (CRWD), Corning (GLW), Bloom Energy (BE), IREN (IREN), USA Rare Earth (USAR), Palo Alto Networks (PANW) and Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE).

Big names in the financial world, including JPMorgan Chase (JPM), Goldman Sachs (GS) and Wells Fargo (WFC), have also raised objections.

Some other prominent names include Walmart (WMT), Coca-Cola (KO), McDonald's (MCD), Eli Lilly (LLY), Adobe (ADBE) and Dell Technologies (DELL).

OKXICE is a joint venture between crypto exchange OKX and Intercontinental Exchange (ICE). Each of them owns a 50% stake in the joint venture.

The goal is to enable tokenized versions of traditional US stocks to be traded on the blockchain.

Instead of buying these shares on a traditional brokerage platform, eligible investors can trade blockchain tokens that represent ownership interests in the underlying securities.

The platform will be open 24 hours a day, seven days a week, as per the company's public notice.

The planned platform will be based on a temporary regulatory exemption issued by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Sept. 17.

However, the regulator gave companies the option to object to any unauthorized third-party tokenization of their shares.

If a company submits an objection within the specified timeframe, then its third-party tokenized shares cannot be offered by the platform under the exemption.

#5319. Dropbox Plans $350M AI Infrastructure Deal With Tigris Buy, Its Biggest Acquisition Yet

Dropbox announced Thursday plans to acquire Tigris Data for $350 million in a transaction the company told Crunchbase News would mark its largest acquisition since its founding in 2007.

Founded by former Uber engineers, Sunnyvale, California-based Tigris is building a network of localized data storage centers that it claims can meet the distributed compute needs of modern AI workloads.

Tigris has raised about $31.9 million since its founding in 2021, per Crunchbase data. Its October 2025 Series A brought in $25 million from lead investor Spark Capital, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz and Basis Set Ventures, which also led its seed round. Other earlier backers include General Catalyst.

Co-founder and CEO Ovais Tariq told TechCrunch at the time of its Series A that the startup had grown 8x every year since its founding in November 2021.

The planned deal would give Dropbox a storage platform built for developers whose applications run across multiple cloud providers.

The acquisition news coincides with what San Francisco-based Dropbox describes as “a significant shift” in its AI strategy as it expands beyond storing and sharing files into selling the infrastructure that companies use to build AI applications.

Publicly traded Dropbox also unveiled DBX Agent Cloud, which will initially offer standalone object storage —  a way to store and retrieve large collections of data, including images, video and the files used to train and run AI models.

For Dropbox, buying Tigris offers a faster route into a market that serves a different audience from the individuals and businesses that use its file-sharing software.

“Tigris brings together a product already running in production, an experienced team, and established relationships with AI developers,” Eric Webster, Dropbox’s chief business officer, told Crunchbase News via email. “That combination would accelerate our entry into infrastructure for AI applications through DBX Agent Cloud.”

Dropbox has made 35 known acquisitions, according to Crunchbase, with much of that activity taking place in its earlier years. Between 2012 and 2015, the company conducted 23 publicly reported acquisitions, including nine in 2014 alone. In contrast, it made four acquisitions across 2024 and 2025, averaging two per year, roughly 65% below its earlier pace.

Its recent purchases suggest a focus on AI-powered productivity, search and security. Dropbox acquired scheduling startup Reclaim.ai and document security company Nira in 2024, followed by Promoted.ai and Mobius Labs in 2025.

While the planned Tigris purchase would be its largest yet, Dropbox has made other sizable purchases over time. Its acquisitions of e-signature company HelloSign in 2019, document-sharing platform DocSend in 2021 and business forms provider FormSwift in 2022 had purchase prices of $230 million, $165 million and $95 million, respectively.

Dropbox’s push into AI infrastructure is one part of a broader strategy that also includes adding AI capabilities to its existing file-sharing product.

For existing customers, the company is bringing AI directly to their Dropbox files to help them find, understand, create, edit and organize content, according to Webster. Customers can switch between supported AI models and work with their Dropbox files in tools like ChatGPT and Claude, with results returning to Dropbox.

For companies and developers, meanwhile, DBX Agent Cloud extends Dropbox’s storage capabilities to the infrastructure behind AI applications and agents.

“DBX Agent Cloud opens a new developer and infrastructure market for Dropbox, while AI inside Dropbox is intended to deepen engagement, retention and expansion among existing customers,” Webster said.

#5318. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

Near Protocol (NEAR): Near $4.40, NEAR has a healthy longer-term chart but must hold $4.00–$4.20 to avoid a deeper correction.

Chainlink is trading at about $11.61, well off its late-September peak near $15.75. On the daily chart, what was a strong bullish run has turned into a corrective consolidation, and right now the price is testing support.

LINK's bullish reversal came in August. It broke above its major moving averages and ran from roughly $8.00 to $15.75. The decline that followed has carved out lower highs and lower lows, and short-term momentum has deteriorated along the way.

The price is now under the shorter-term moving averages, which are bunched around $12.00–$12.60, so sellers still control the near-term trend. Still, LINK is holding above its 200-day moving average near $11.00, and as long as it does, the wider recovery stays intact.

The first support is $11.40–$11.50. Below that sits $11.00, a psychological level. If that gives way for good, the $10.40–$10.60 region comes into view; buyers showed up there recently.

Resistance starts near $12.00–$12.20, and the $12.50–$12.70 supply zone above it is the stronger barrier. Win those back, and a recovery toward $13.30 starts to look more likely.

Daily RSI is around 40–45, on the weak side of neutral. Buying momentum is subdued, but LINK isn't deeply oversold.

There was a sharp wick down toward $10.30 recently, and the price climbed back above $11.50 afterward. That could mean demand is soaking up the selling. One rejection candle doesn't confirm a reversal, though.

Short term, LINK looks neutral to bearish. Its next real move will probably be decided by the $11.00 support and the $12.20–$12.70 resistance zone.

NEAR Protocol trades near $4.40. It had a big rally off its August range of $1.60–$1.80, and even after the latest pullback the bigger structure still looks healthy. Short-term momentum is fading, though, so it may need to consolidate for a while before the next sustained leg up.

#5315. Exclusive: Nurx And Journey Clinical Co-Founders Raise $6M For Mental Health Startup Siggy

Siggy has raised $6 million in pre-seed funding to build a mental health service that uses AI to collect patients’ histories and track progress between appointments with licensed clinicians, the startup told Crunchbase News exclusively.

The company brings together two founders who previously built businesses that help patients get treatment outside a traditional doctor’s office. Jonathan Sabbagh co-founded Journey Clinical, which supports practices offering ketamine-assisted psychotherapy, and Edvard Engesæth co-founded Nurx, which provides birth control and other healthcare services online.

Village Global led the financing for New York-based Siggy. Notably, several investors in the round previously backed one or both founders. They include Albert Wenger of Union Square Ventures, Mercury co-founder Immad Akhund, and Cityblock Health co-founder Toyin Ajayi, through Coalition Operators. Other participants include PsyMed Ventures, Mystic Ventures and Gokul Rajaram.

The founders said they began building Siggy in late 2025. The round, which they plan to use to hire more clinicians and engineers, develop the software and work on regulatory requirements,

is the first outside funding for the company. The startup recently began accepting paying patients ahead of its public launch, and the founders said they next plan to test the service with paying patients before expanding further.

Sabbagh, Siggy’s CEO, told Crunchbase News in an interview that the company is addressing a problem he encountered in mental healthcare. Therapists and the clinicians prescribing their patients’ medication often work separately. Patients may see a therapist weekly but have only a brief appointment every few months with their prescriber. This leaves little time or opportunity to discuss changes in symptoms or medication side effects.

To address that problem, Siggy uses AI conversations and daily check-ins to gather information clinicians can review between visits.

“AI helps maintain the conversation and organize what patients share, so clinicians have a richer picture of the person that they’re treating,” said Engesæth, the startup’s COO, in an interview.

Patients begin by answering questions about their history through a free AI conversation. They then meet a licensed clinician by video, who reviews that information. The clinician then makes a diagnosis and prescribes medication if appropriate.

Patients can talk with Siggy’s AI between appointments and can also check in each day to report their sleep, mood, medication and how they feel physically. The company combines those answers with data from connected wearable devices to produce a daily “Siggy Score” out of 100. The score is visible to both the patient and clinician.

Patients can opt to connect wearables such as Whoop, Oura or Apple Watch, adding sleep, activity, heart rate and heart rate variability data to the daily check-ins that underpin the Siggy Score. The company aims to use those patterns to flag difficult stretches earlier, including when patients report feeling fine despite worsening sleep or other physical changes.

If the score changes, the software flags it for a clinician to review. Patients also receive weekly check-ins during their first eight weeks of treatment, according to the company.

Clinicians decide whether to continue treatment or adjust medication, and also handle all medical questions. When appropriate, they can help patients taper off gradually. Siggy does not prescribe controlled substances and is not a crisis service, the founders said.

One important note: Patients can continue seeing their existing therapists while using Siggy, Sabbagh said. A planned feature would let patients share information with other providers and involve loved ones in their care.

As with many startup founders, Sabbagh’s interest in mental health treatment grew out of his own experience. After two decades in finance, he experienced burnout and was eventually diagnosed with PTSD related to childhood trauma. He said ketamine-assisted therapy helped him recover, leading him to return to school to study psychology at 38.

He subsequently co-founded Journey Clinical. Sabbagh said he has since become its executive chairman, remaining involved while taking on the CEO role at Siggy.

Engesæth, a physician by training, was an early investor in Journey and advised Sabbagh as he built the company.

Before that, Engesæth co-founded Nurx, which initially helped patients obtain birth control prescriptions and receive medication at home. He said the company grew to more than 2 million patients and an annual revenue run rate exceeding $100 million before merging with Thirty Madison in 2022.

The two had considered starting a company together for years. With Siggy, they say they want to make the regular contact and coordination Sabbagh had with his own providers available to more patients.

Siggy accepts commercial insurance in all 50 states and is expanding into government insurance programs. Patients can also pay directly; insured patients’ costs vary by plan.

Insurance was a priority because many prospective patients cannot afford treatment out of pocket, Engesæth said. The founders also say Siggy’s service will be permanently free to veterans.

Amrit Rao, a general partner at Village Global, told Crunchbase News via email that the founders’ experience building healthcare companies was a major reason he invested.

The fact that Siggy accepts insurance was important too. “Pairing that vision with an insurance-based model makes the ambition about access as much as technology,” he said.

Mercury co-founder and CEO Immad Akhund, who invested personally, is a repeat backer of both founders.  He pointed to their longer-term ambition of using AI to understand each patient’s brain health well enough to detect changes early.

“That’s why I’m backing them again with Siggy,” he added, “and why I’m excited to be in early on what they build next.”

#5314. 40 Million XRP Moved From Binance Hacker Wallet

Blockchain tracking service Whale Alert has reported that a wallet linked to the massive $6.3 billion Binance hack has just sent 40 million XRP (~$50.5 million) to a mystery address.

On Nov. 2, Whale Alert shared information about the huge XRP transfer, noting that the transaction initiator is an address tagged "Binance Hack 2026."

The huge transfer took place at 03:56 UTC, Whale Alert data shows. The transaction involved 40 million XRP (~$50.46 million).

Interestingly, just 50 seconds before that, Whale Alert reported another transfer of 40 million XRP.

Another 40 million XRP (~$50.44 million) was also sent from the wallet tagged as "Binance Hack 2026" to a mystery address.

In total, these two transfers involved 80 million XRP (~$100.9 million).

Both transfers originated from the same wallet but were sent to separate mystery addresses.

It is still unclear why these transfers were made. There is no sign that these funds have been sent to a crypto exchange or sold yet.

The transactions took place just days after Binance faced one of the biggest cryptocurrency hacks ever.

The massive XRP transfers came shortly after Binance started to restore cryptocurrency withdrawals following the unprecedented security breach the cryptocurrency exchange faced.

On Nov. 1, Binance annonced that the exchange would restore withdrawals in phases for 15 blockchain networks, including XRP Ledger, Bitcoin, Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain and Solana.

It also mentioned that withdrawals would be gradually restored for other networks, such as Tron, Dogecoin, Zcash, Avalanche, Sui, Polygon and Arbitrum.

The first stage of withdrawal resumption was set to take place between 06:00 and 09:00 UTC on Nov. 1.

After Binance faced a security breach on Oct. 29, which led to the loss of around $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrency from its hot wallets, it temporarily paused withdrawals.

The exchange noted that withdrawals would be restored gradually after the security and infrastructure checks had been performed.

Binance also said that XRP balances were already fully backed, as were those of other major cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and BNB.

Binance claimed that, as of Nov. 1, around 95% of affected assets had been replenished. The remaining 5% consists primarily of less liquid cryptocurrencies.

#5313. Hackers Use Claude, Gemini and Kimi to Identify Valuable Crypto Targets

Cybercriminals are using popular artificial intelligence (AI) models like Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini and Moonshot AI's Kimi AI to evaluate the financial worth of potential victims, including those owning cryptocurrencies.

Cybersecurity researchers at Cisco Talos detailed in a new report how a new type of Windows malware dubbed VOLTA-AUTODOXER, or simply VOLTA, steals sensitive data and uses AI tools to identify potentially lucrative targets among compromised users.

Compared to traditional information-stealing malware, which mainly steals passwords and credentials, VOLTA can also analyze stolen data to build victim profiles and determine what assets hackers can potentially exploit for profit.

Notably, one of VOLTA's most dangerous features is its ability to extract sensitive crypto wallet information, including recovery seed phrases, which can potentially give attackers access to digital assets.

VOLTA also includes features that can crack cryptocurrency wallet vaults, posing a big risk for people who store their crypto wallet credentials on their computers.

But its features are not just limited to stealing crypto.

As explained by Cisco Talos security researcher Ryan Fetterman, VOLTA can also grab saved browser passwords, payment card info, authentication tokens, email credentials and active sessions on popular platforms like Telegram, Discord, Steam and Roblox.

It can also extract info from Outlook accounts and Slack workspaces, as well as other personal and professional information on the infected system.

The malware also takes things further by analyzing victims' email accounts to grab more personal data.

For example, it can scan Gmail accounts for purchase confirmations and receipts from services like Amazon, PayPal, Walmart, DoorDash and Uber Eats.

This way, attackers can get more details about a victim's identity, home address, job and spending habits.

The malware can send stolen data to AI models via the OpenRouter service, which provides access to several AI models.

It first tries to process the collected data using Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6.

If the model fails to process the request, VOLTA is hardcoded to try Moonshot AI's Kimi K2 and Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash.

As explained by Cisco Talos, VOLTA specifically looks for refusal responses before attempting to use a different AI model.

It feeds the collected data to the AI models and asks them to analyze it, providing a comprehensive evaluation of a victim's financial worth.

It can also help identify valuable assets and then rank them based on how lucrative they may be. It can also score a victim's cybersecurity.

Essentially, it allows hackers to use AI models to find potentially lucrative targets without the need to manually sift through stolen data.

#5311. XRP Final Move: Binance Empties Hacked Wallet of Last $101 Million

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions.
